one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 6, 2024 as closing remarks at the FLP Professorial Chair lecture at De La Salle University BGC's Tañada-Diokno School of Law, this speech by CJP opens with two institutional corrections: first, the school name should be Diokno-Tañada (alphabetically, since both are deemed equal in honors); second, Dean Gil De Los Reyes need not apologize for praying, since the Constitution's Preamble is itself 'an express prayer to God' and the 'Prayer for the Courts' composed in 2001 is still prayed before every SC session. CJP introduces MBF Secretary Chito Sobrepeña and wife Anna Sobrepeña, MBF EVP Dr. Boyet Dy, FLP Trustee DJ De Jesus, and youngest FLP Trustee Atty. Arvin Cortez (founding FLP Scholars Society president). He presents Dean Chel Diokno his P150,000 stipend (less 10% withholding tax), calling his lecture 'one of the best, if not the best' of the 17 FLP series to date. He then pays tribute to Chel as the 'worthy son of a worthy father' -- his father Senator Jose W. Diokno, one of CJP's three idol-lawyers (along with Salonga and Teehankee): JWD was a bar-exam topnotcher (tied with Salonga) despite not completing the four-year law course (taught by his SC Justice father), and founding chair of the Commission on Human Rights. CJP narrates his unforgettable courtroom story: a sick Salonga sent the young CJP to a hearing before Judge Mojica in old CFI Pasay; JWD, as opposing counsel, graciously asked for a postponement 'in fairness to my young compañero' -- 'I was shaking in my boots, although I did not want to show it.' On substance, CJP adds to Dean Diokno's human-rights lecture by proposing that big-time investors (not just companies) be convinced to require the PRR of human rights as an investment condition, and banks to lend only to human-rights-compliant companies -- distinguishing genuine human rights under the rule of law from those under the 'rule of one' in authoritarian regimes. He closes by endorsing peaceful settlement and ADR as the judiciary-mandated business-dispute mode, and expressing the wish that Chel will one day become a Senator: 'Marami kang admirers dito, Chel.'

He expresses regret at missing the Grand Dinner in honor of retired CJ Hatta Ali, thanks CJ Syarifuddin for his hospitality, and invites him to visit the Philippines on a goodwill mission to meet ALA Philippines members and the incumbent SC members. He introduces the Philippine delegation of over a dozen jurists, lawyers, and academics -- asking them to open their cameras and wave online -- and expresses anticipation at hearing the reports on the ALA Institute, the ALA Guidelines on Best Practices to Enforce Arbitral Awards within ASEAN, the ASLOM update, and the Working Group reports. one_paragraph_summary: Written August 18-27, 2022 as the Exordium (Latin for Introduction) to Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna's autobiography, this piece by CJP opens with the 6:51 AM SMS: Azcuna asked CJP to 'do me the honor of an Exordium'; CJP read the 50,265-word, 271-page final draft in six hours over the August 20-21 weekend. CJP describes the autobiography as 'simple and graspable; humble and palpable; never haughty or naughty or deprecating, yet no less ennobling and enabling,' and argues for calling Azcuna 'The Consummate Constitutionalist' -- a title justified by three simultaneous distinctions: constitution maker (1971 ConCon delegate for Lone District of Zamboanga del Norte, age 32, where four of his proposals -- bar integration, citizen's army, continental shelf, and the writ of Amparo -- were debated; the first three passed but Amparo had to wait for the 1987 Constitution, where with Concepcion's advice it was inserted into Art. VIII on Judicial Power); constitution implementer (Chief Presidential Legal Counsel, Press Secretary, and other Cory-era roles -- surviving coup attempts, advising Cory she could run in 1992 but would graciously decline); and constitution interpreter (SC Associate Justice, appointed by GMA October 20, 2002). CJP highlights three passages from the book: Rina Azcuna's child-definition of a lawyer ('A LAWYER IS SOMEONE WHO HELPS THE JUDGE FIND OUT WHAT REALLY HAPPENED' -- 'the best definition of a lawyer,' CJP agrees); the simplified EEZ explanation (pages 134-136: sovereign rights but not sovereignty, 200 nautical miles, UNCLOS-governed); and Bayan v. Ermita -- 'his most remarkable decision' -- creating 'freedom parks, either real or constructive, all over the country.' CJP also recalls his personal role in securing the P300-million no-strings Japanese government grant for the PHILJA Training Center in Tagaytay (January 18, 2006, check presented by Ambassador Yamamoto at the SC Session Hall). The Exordium closes: 'We never retire. We just change tires for a new journey' -- with a prediction that in ten years CJP will crown Azcuna 'The Consummate Hubby, Dad and Lolo,' even from a wheelchair.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered on October 18, 2019 at New World Hotel Makati at a tribute dinner sponsored by the Makati Business Club, MAP, and FINEX, this is Panganiban's eyewitness biography of Antonio T. Carpio's five missed chances at the Chief Justiceship across his 18-year Supreme Court career. The first chance (May 2010, post-Puno) was declined for 'delicadeza' -- Carpio had voted against the midnight-appointment decision authorizing the very vacancy, refusing to be 'Mr. Midnight Chief Justice'; the chiefship went to Corona. The second (May 2012, post-Corona impeachment) was lost when Aquino III told Carpio directly that he admired his qualifications but key Senate allies and three business leaders opposed him. The third (post-Sereno quo warranto) was again declined for delicadeza -- Carpio had dissented from the ouster decision; De Castro got the post. The Court unanimously granted Carpio CJ-level salary and retirement benefits. Panganiban frames the 'best news' as still to come: when China accedes to the rule of law over the West Philippine Sea, Carpio's single-minded advocacy will earn him acclamation as 'a hero and a patriot.' Panganiban interleaves Carpio's near-resignation with him over Lambino vs Comelec (2006) and Carpio's last-minute Edsa 2 pleading that made Arroyo regular rather than Acting President. one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 10, 2019 at the launch of the Ateneo Law Journal special edition honoring CJ Claudio Teehankee's 100th birthday, this speech by CJP -- on behalf of the Claudio Teehankee Foundation -- opens with two self-deprecating octogenarian jokes: Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer transformed at age 80 into 'the senility prayer' ('Lord, grant me the senility to forget the people I never liked'), and Frank Laubach's 'Life Begins at 80' ('at 70, people are mad at you for everything; at 80, you have a perfect excuse'). The substantive argument draws a sharp distinction between bar exam excellence (memorization: 'read and reread... till the words are erased from the pages' -- producing 'mere legal robots who parrot laws and decisions word-for-word') and law journal editing and writing (analysis, criticism and improvisation -- producing 'social engineers who view the law not as an end by itself, but as an instrument in the building of a just society'). CJ Teehankee embodies the synthesis: summa cum laude and bar topnotcher, but not merely a legal technician -- 'he was a social engineer who reached out to the stars to render justice via the all-encompassing rule of law,' a courageous national hero deservingly buried at Libingan ng mga Bayani. CJP notes the Ateneo Law Journal holds a special place in his heart, having written Forewords twice -- once for Lead Editor Jewelle Santos (also a Teehankee Foundation scholar) and once for Lead Editor Angelo Herbosa. He closes by linking FLP's dissertation writing contest (25 prizes from P20,000 to P300,000) to this same social-engineering aspiration: training law students to become, alongside bar topnotchers, 'social engineers who construct durable and unbreakable institutions for the nation.'

one_paragraph_summary: Published March 9, 2019 as interview responses by CJP about the Manila Cathedral coffee table book ('Restoring a Monument to Faith, Architecture and History'), this document covers two questions. On how the idea started: the restoration of the Manila Cathedral began in 2010 when Cardinal Rosales summoned the Manila Metropolitan Cathedral-Basilica Foundation (CJP as President) to address the swaying belfry; structural engineers found not just the belfry but the entire edifice needed strengthening; and to CJP's dismay, no as-built plans were found anywhere (not in Archdiocese archives, the National Library, or the Manila City Engineer's Office), with the additional alarm that the Cathedral was built on reclaimed land that 'could liquefy and cause the Cathedral to collapse.' When Cardinal Tagle succeeded Rosales, CJP advised him (with others) that closing the Cathedral was legally necessary to avoid liability should it collapse -- making it Tagle's first major decision as Archbishop. After the four Rs were completed with the Lord's guidance, CJP proposed a coffee table book to document the restoration with structural and architectural plans -- 'so that 50 years or 100 years from now, future generations who may wish to re-strengthen, retrofit and re-beautify the Cathedral will no longer meet the same baffling problems we faced.' The Board (chaired by Cardinal Tagle, vice-chaired by Ambassador Tita de Villa) welcomed the proposal; Metrobank Foundation had exhausted its budget; referred it to the GT Foundation; Alfred Ty 'gallantly and kindly agreed at short notice' and personally delivered the check on the day of the interview. Under Dr. Gerald Lico's design and editing, the book 'metamorphosed into a world-class, grand coffee table book' distributed worldwide. On the book's legacy: 'More than brick and mortar, the Manila Cathedral is a symbol of our deep faith and a monument of our religious heritage as a people... the coffee table book is a testament not just to the herculean effort to restore... but a witness to the architectural and historical genius of our faithful in their adoration of our Lord and in their veneration of our Lady.'

one_paragraph_summary: Written August 1, 2018 as the Foreword to the Ateneo Law Journal at the request of Lead Editor Angelo Francesco F. Herbosa, this piece by CJP advances the 'disruptive symphony' thesis: the volume's 10 apparently disparate articles are united by a single arching theme -- disruption -- with their very disparateness as 'the arching melody itself.' He comments on seven articles: Diokno's ('Now or Never') traces how the justice system was 'robbed of its independence and integrity by an unwanted dictatorship' and offers reform solutions; Candelaria-Balisong on Republic v. Sereno treats it as the Court 'consolidating its power to exact accountability even from its own leader'; Santiago-Pelongco (to be read together with Candelaria-Balisong) dissects the ponencia's 'apparent misuse of a remedy found only in the Rules of Court to undermine a constitutional remedy historically intended as the only method to oust impeachable officials.' CJP's sharpest intervention is his forward-looking question on Sereno: when the Court's composition changes and most incumbents retire, will the decision withstand a petition declaring it void for 'being rendered without due process by a biased majority who apparently had not only prejudged their Chief but in fact conceived the very weapon of quo warranto to oust her?' -- potentially enabling Sereno's return as 'the first woman to head the highest court of the land.' Sta. Maria's foreign divorce article (Van Dorn to Manalo) exposes Article 26 of the Family Code as 'zigzagged by the Supreme Court, in the process succumbing to judicial legislation in the guise of interpretation'; Calleja tackles the Marcos v. Robredo 50%-vs-25% shading threshold; Mata-Perez on TRAIN 1 prompts CJP's sole policy intervention: 'Why is the government raising new revenue streams when infrastructure could be built through PPP agreements?' The technology trio -- WTO (Baguilat), online child exploitation (Aritao-Pangilinan), Data Privacy Act (Pardu-Jacob) -- is praised as examining 'the most disruptive phenomenon of our time: technology,' prompting CJP's call that 'law, lawmakers, magistrates and lawyers must keep pace with the speedy march of science.' He closes by honoring Herbosa's team as future 'topnotch advocates and eminent justices': 'My wish is to live long enough to witness their passage.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 27, 2014 at the 25th Death Anniversary commemoration of CJ Claudio Teehankee, this address by CJP delivers three messages. First, thanks to the Claudio Teehankee Foundation for conferring on him the Rule of Law Award on April 13, 2013 and inviting him to join its Board of Trustees. He greets CJ Hilario Davide Jr. (Foundation chairman and CJP's predecessor, whose Action Program for Judicial Reform 'became the exemplar or model of the World Bank in judicial reforms,' a program CJP continued), Justice Arturo Brion (Ateneo valedictorian and bar topnotcher like Teehankee), and Ambassador Manuel Dondi Teehankee ('worthy son of the worthy father'). Second, tribute to Teehankee: summa cum laude in both preparatory law and LLB from 'the best university in the Philippines'; his mentor Salonga warned whenever facing Teehankee: 'You better prepare our trial brief very well because we are going to be on the opposite side of one of the best lawyers in town.' Teehankee pioneered the libertarian philosophy, 'nearly died for it,' was bypassed twice for CJ under Marcos ('it is easy to be brave during peace time like now, but during the Martial Law years, there were many gifted public officials but few had the courage to stand up for their convictions'), and was finally appointed 16th CJ by Cory Aquino in 1986. Spotting Oscar Lopez at the back of the auditorium, CJP extends the same tribute to the Lopez Group, which 'stood up against President Marcos... undaunted and stood up for dignity, honor and country.' Third, the FLP-Teehankee Foundation kindredship: Teehankee's libertarian philosophy is embedded in the Constitution; FLP extends it to economic freedom -- 'it is not just the political liberty of our people that we must serve, protect and promote. We must also serve, protect and promote economic freedom.' Businessmen who benefit most from free enterprise 'have the obligation to share their benefits with their workers and their fellow Filipinos, so we can all conquer poverty and ultimately share prosperity.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 26, 2014 at the Philippine Bar Association's monthly luncheon fellowship at the Tower Club, Makati -- CJP accepting due to gratitude for the PBA's 2007 Award of Honor -- this address surveys four rapidly changing domains (communications: from land lines to Viber, Skype and social media, ending in the prediction that 'newspapers, land lines, movie houses, the post office and even our constitutionally-protected privacy will disappear'; medicine: from healing to preventing to longevity to 'eternity' via stem cells; business: proprietorships to multinationals more powerful than governments; politics: monarchy to liberal democracy born from Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death'). He notes the jurisprudential tension: the SC showed 'vigor and vitality in promoting political rights' in Disini v. Sec. of Justice (Cybercrimes, Feb 2014); he wishes the same would be shown for economic rights. His Tanada v. Angara (May 1997) ponencia is presented as the definitive answer: strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation on economic matters; private enterprise as the engine; the economic pie must be enlarged, not just divided. He comments on Manila Prince v. GSIS (Manila Hotel; CJP dissented), Gamboa v. Teves (40% foreign ownership in utilities limited to voting shares -- urges prospective application), and Initiatives for Dialogue v. PSALM (river water nationalized but private once dammed). The textualist-vs-living-Constitution debate is illustrated with the Scalia-Kennedy anecdote. The substantive reform proposal: Rule 138's restriction on bar admission to Filipinos and Philippine residents is outdated given ASEAN 2015 integration, 10 million OFWs ($26 billion) and 1 million BPO workers ($16 billion); Dean Bautista's Hopewell-Clifford Chance example (Hong Kong developer, New York-law loans, fly-in-fly-out lawyers) shows the rule's inadequacy under Cayetano v. Monsod's expansive practice-of-law definition. CJP proposes four conditions for allowing limited foreign practice. He closes with an ethics charge -- shysters who deliberately delay cases and prosecutors who file baseless charges ('not only unethical, it is brazenly criminal') -- and three calls: rededication to competent and ethical practice; fresh look at globalizing political and economic rights; and for the legal profession to help safeguard liberty AND conquer poverty AND nurture prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 30, 2012 as the Guest of Honor address at the program marking the 113th Anniversary of the Historic Siege of Baler and the 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day -- invited by Senator Edgardo J. Angara ('best trained and most well rounded potential President the Philippines will ever have'; IBP President 1979; ALA founding president 1980; longest serving senator) -- this address by CJP presents three milestones. The Siege of Baler: on June 28, 1898, Katipuneros launched an uprising; 50 Spanish cazadores under Capitan Enrique de las Morenas retreated to the stone-walled Baler parish church; unaware that the Spanish-American War had already changed the geopolitical context (poor communications), they held for 337 days before surrendering June 2, 1899 with only one officer and 30 soldiers alive; brought to Tarlac, they were 'treated with admiration for their bravery and dedication to their duty'; on June 30, 1899 -- exactly 113 years before this speech -- President Aguinaldo issued a presidential decree directing that Cerezo and his men be deemed 'not as prisoners but as friends,' praising 'the valor, constancy and heroism with which that handful of isolated men, without any hope of help, defended their banner for a period of one year.' CJP derives four virtues of Baler: 'bravery in battle; honor in capitulation; friendship in victory; and progress in peace -- these four virtues characterize every great nation and every great leader.' Second milestone: the 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day, now a relationship of 'equal and sovereign partners in the world.' Third milestone: the bicentennial of the Cadiz Constitution (March 19, 1812) -- enacted while the Spanish Cortes was on retreat from Napoleon; 37 of its 303 representatives were from overseas territories; signed for the Philippines by Ventura de los Reyes of Vigan; established limited monarchy, popular sovereignty, universal male suffrage, freedom of the press and private property -- and, critically, recognized Philippine representation in Spanish lawmaking. CJP cites historians who consider it 'our first sovereign charter,' predating the Biak-na-Bato, Malolos, 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions. He also notes Spain's lasting legal legacy: the Penal Code, Civil Code and Code of Commerce.

Hilbay of the UP Institute of Government and Law Reform -- this address by CJP opens with a formal disclosure: 'I have been sitting as an independent member of the board of advisers of PLDT since mid-2009... I do not represent PLDT's management or any stockholder. I cannot propose or second motions. Neither can I vote.' That is most cruel and unfair.' His proposed remedies: give investors a few years to comply if the decision cannot be reversed; and Congress should pass a new law governing an orderly and fair divestment process.

Comelec decision -- analyzes the system through three landmark cases. Veterans (1998): CJP devised the 'Panganiban formula' (informally christened by textwriters) for allocating party-list seats based on four inviolable parameters: (1) 20% allocation; (2) 2% threshold; (3) three-seat limit; (4) proportional representation. Comelec (April 2009): in 'one fell swoop' increased party-list seats from 22 to 55 (total congressmen from 238 to 271); upheld the 2% threshold for the initial guaranteed seat but declared unconstitutional the second clause of Section 11(b) of the Party-List Law which gave additional seats proportionally to those above 2% -- this 'radically changed the rules of the game'; any party, 'regardless of how few its votes were,' can now get a Congressional seat; the Buhay (7.33% of votes, three seats) vs. Cocofed (0.98%, one seat) comparison shows 'grave violence to the precept of proportional representation.' The 2010 Comelec was applying 'inconsistent standards... sometimes outrightly contrary to jurisprudence' on accreditation despite nine years of clear Ang Bagong Bayani guidance. Conclusion: 'the party-list system is clearly vulnerable to manipulation and misuse... may be readily co-opted and utilized to maintain certain personages in political power. The clarion call of the hour is for ceaseless public vigilance and amendatory legislation.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 26, 2010 as keynote speaker and inducting officer at the MAP 2010 Board of Governors induction -- on the MAP theme 'Principled Leadership in Challenging Times' -- this address by CJP (a former MAP Board member from 1990-1994) presents the TIP framework: Trust, Integrity and Probity. He opens with an archbishop's homily unpacking 'love thy neighbor' into its justice dimension: 'Shall we just feed the hungry but not punish the greedy who deprived them of food? Shall we just provide clothing without chasing the robbers who stole the clothes?' He distinguishes three kinds of government officials: (1) those who arrogate power and plunder; (2) those who are personally pure under abusive regimes -- honesty being 'a virtue taught in grade school'; (3) those with integrity who have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants' -- what the country needs in challenging times. On trust: the Philippines went from the envy of Asia in the 1950s (P2 = $1) to the backwater of Asia (almost P50 = $1, 'the exchange rate has sunk more than 20 times in 50 years'). Those who propose Singapore-style authoritarianism are wrong -- 'the Philippines is not Singapore; during the martial law years, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.' The proof: 'Look at the Filipinos abroad. They strictly follow the law. They stop at red lights even in deserted street corners. They honor their obligations. They pay their taxes willingly.' In democratic societies like the US and Canada, Filipinos flourish -- because 'in a democracy, the essence of good governance is the trust of the people.' On probity: Webster's 'uncompromising adherence to the highest principles or ideals,' plus CJP's addition -- 'the ability to discern alternatives and select the best' -- in short, 'do the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons.' He recombines the three values into the TIP mnemonic ('my TIP on how to meet the challenges of these times') and closes with Jesus washing his disciples' feet at the Last Supper: 'I have given you a model to follow... leading by example is the best, if not the only, way to long-term and effective leadership.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 27, 2009 as keynote at the First Integrity and Human Rights Conference -- chaired by Leila de Lima (CHR Chairperson); co-speakers include Loida Nicolas-Lewis (Bisyon 2020; 'She and I have been involved in nation-building since our college days as organizers and officers of NUSP') -- this address presents a data-driven indictment of the Arroyo administration's governance record. World Bank data: control of corruption fell from 45% in 1996 (Ramos) to 22% in 2007 (GMA) -- 'we edged out Indonesia for the dubious title of being the most corrupt nation in East Asia.' Transparency International ranked the Philippines 121st (2006) → 131st (2007) → 141st (2008), 'well below Mongolia (102), Nigeria (115), Ethiopia and Indonesia (both 126). Somalia, the notorious home of pirates in Africa, was rated the most corrupt at 180th place.' Pulse Asia: GMA 42% most corrupt; 71% of business managers bribed. Karapatan documented 977 EJKs, 1,010 torture victims, 1,464 illegal arrests across eight Arroyo years. CHR Chair de Lima: the record is 'dismal.' The response from leaders: 'mostly rhetoric, evasiveness and finger-pointing, like calling TI biased and suggesting it had been bought by the opposition.' CJP's diagnosis: 'we have enough laws and enough democratic institutions... What is needed is leadership by example by the President, the Ombudsman's exercise of independence and diligence, and the COA's dogged insistence on accountability.' The root problem: 'society has bastardized ethics into public relations techniques. Such duplicity is fundamentally flawed. Pretension is really a source of anxiety and frustration.' Two solutions: (1) strict enforcement of the Ethical Standards Law; (2) strengthen democratic institutions -- 'the citizens' job is to perform oversight functions: to demand that only the most qualified are elected or appointed, and then to insist that these public officials perform their duties ethically, courageously and competently.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 8, 2008 as the tone-setting keynote at the GAJE (Global Alliance of Justice Education) 5th Worldwide Conference in the Philippines, this address by CJP opens with Obama's election as 'a major milestone in the battle for human dignity and equality that started with the adoption of the Magna Charta by the British, carried on by all independence-loving peoples, to the French Revolution, and then to America where human freedom was immortalized in the Bill of Rights.' He situates the Philippines in this history (all Constitutions enshrine the Bill of Rights; the Constitution mandates 'a just and dynamic social order to free the people from poverty'). He proposes two projects for the GAJE conference: (1) The ICC -- founded July 17, 1998 (120 states at the Rome Diplomatic Conference; effective July 1, 2002 with 60 ratifications); fights the impunity of dictators and heads of state 'who could not be sued in their home countries due to national immunity from suit' for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. (2) PERLAS (Public Education on the Rule of Law) -- 'which in Filipino and Spanish means a pearl of great price'; teaches the basics of democracy, rule of law, justice and peace at the basic school level; workbooks and teaching exemplars already developed and printed, ready for Philippine elementary and high schools. The governing political philosophy: 'in many places, we still have rulers who practice authoritarianism... on the opposite extreme, regimes where mobs and charlatans abuse democratic processes. The solution to both extremes is the rule of law. No one should be so powerful, so moneyed or so influential as to be above the law.' He closes with a new-paradigm enumeration: 'mix these mantras with the cyber-age and globalization, and we come face to face with new paradigms of justice like mediation in lieu of litigation, public interest law centers, international bridges to justice, independent commissions on human rights, writs of amparo and, if I may stress, the International Criminal Court and PERLAS, the pearl of a great price.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 8, 2008 at the CIDA Asia Field Representatives Meeting -- CIDA having arranged the 2002 Ottawa visit and the JURIS (Judicial Reform Initiative Support Project) MOU signing -- this address by CJP centers on the most memorable episode of his judicial career: the June 18, 2002 lunch at the Supreme Court of Canada, hosted by CJ Beverley McLachlin in the Judges' Dining Room. The Philippine delegation (CJ Davide, Justice Herrera and CJP) was challenged by Senior Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dubé, who noted that Philippine decisions liberally cite Holmes, Black and Frankfurter 'but I have yet to see one that cites our Canadian justices.' CJP replied honestly: 'I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court.' He 'took the banter to heart': upon returning, he penned People v. Genosa -- 'adopting for the first time the battered woman syndrome as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a prosecution for parricide' -- and expressly cited a Canadian SC decision as authority. 'That encounter may have been a minor incident in the great history of the Canadian Court, but it was a major event of my judicial career.' He presents his vision-mission as CJ: four Ins (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence); impervious to the 'plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship'; four ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay); twin goals of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law. He closes with Pierre Elliott Trudeau's 'just society' as the Canadian analog -- defined by McLachlin at her Ateneo honorary doctorate speech as 'a society governed by the rule of law and built on the values of democracy, equality and liberty... where all can participate, where all can pursue a dream, where all enjoy basic liberties of expression, association and movement' -- and thanks CIDA for sharing this vision with the Philippines.

one_paragraph_summary: Published April 29, 2008 as the outline or lecture notes for a presentation titled 'The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint,' this document by CJP is structured as topic labels with brief descriptions rather than a full speech transcript. It begins with the Eisenhower-liberal-duo framing (CJ Earl Warren and Justice William Brennan as Eisenhower's unintended activist appointees). It covers the major sources of Philippine law (constitutional, political, commercial and remedial law; civil and criminal law), the Philippine governmental structure (separation of powers), and the definition of judicial power under Section 1 Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution: (1) settling actual controversies involving legally demandable rights; (2) determining grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. The definition of grave abuse of discretion is given in full: 'Capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment by reason of passion or personal hostility in a manner so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined, or to act at all in contemplation of law. Also, any action done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence.' The outline compares the Philippine grave-abuse-of-discretion jurisdiction with the US political question doctrine. It lists ten measures guaranteeing judicial independence: fiscal autonomy; security of tenure and compensation; protection from removal; non-diminution of powers; administrative supervision over lower courts; continuing judicial education; freedom from congressional confirmation; control of bar admission; rule-making power; and protection and enforcement of constitutional rights. It closes with the ACID problems (Access, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay) and the four-Ins vision (Independence, Integrity, Industry, Intelligence) safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 15, 2007 as the keynote at the NUSP 36th National Student Congress -- the 50th anniversary of the NUSP's founding -- this address by CJP opens with the most candid personal preference statement in the corpus: 'I have lived on this planet for over seventy years; have met some of the most important people that populate it; have traveled to all the continents of our earth, except Antarctica. Yet let me tell you very candidly that I would exchange all of that to turn back the hands of time and to relive my years as a student leader.' He narrates the NUSP founding: in September 1957, as the newly elected FEU CSO president, CJP questioned the communist and partisan activities in SCAP and CONDA; SCAP tried to placate him by unanimously electing him VP for International Affairs (free travel, Malacañang pocket money); 'notwithstanding all these, I chose the more difficult, straight and narrow path by seceding from both the SCAP and CONDA, rejecting my lucrative position in SCAP, and refusing membership in the President's august Little Cabinet.' Student leaders from UP, UST, San Beda, St. Theresa's, National University and Sta. Isabel joined the walk-out, forming the NUSP nucleus. The founding vision: 'pledged to unite and reflect faithfully student opinion on current national issues, free the youth from undue political interferences, fight communist infiltration in the campuses, and redirect the youth's thinking and energy to constructive idealism.' Core values: dignity, integrity, independence, liberty, responsibility, democracy. Achievements: 'the communist effort to infiltrate student movements failed; freedom prevailed; and the students were liberated from the political and partisan apron strings of the government.' For today's students: tackle the present plagues (poverty, malgovernance, corruption, EJKs); have a vision and values; 'put them in writing and include them in your digital files, so that fifty years from now, in the presence of your children and grandchildren, you may show these mementos and declare before God and man that you have lived your life in accordance with these cherished ideals.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 26, 2007 at the PBA's 116th Foundation Day -- the day after 1,893 lawyers from the 2006 bar were sworn in at the PICC -- this address by CJP (in his first months as a retired CJ) provides a comprehensive data-driven review of the 2006 bar and the state of legal education. The 2006 bar has several historic firsts: the largest-ever batch (6,187 takers); topnotcher Noel Neil Q. Malimba from the University of the Cordilleras; Ateneo's Ricardo Pilares Jr. and UP's Deborah Acosta tied for second; FEU's Gina Lyn Rubio took fifth; and for the first time, four non-Metro Manila schools (UC, University of San Carlos, Romualdez Educational Foundation, University of Cebu) made the top ten. Bar illustrados among sitting SC members: Carpio (6th, 1975), Azcuna (4th, 1962), Velasco (6th, 1971), Nachura (7th, 1967). Of 21 past CJs, nine were topnotchers -- including Pedro Yap (1st, 1946), Narvasa (2nd, 1951) and CJP himself (6th, 1960). School performance (1946-2006): UP produced 25 number ones; Ateneo 17; San Beda 6; FEU 4. Passing rates (1991-2005): Ateneo 87.57%, San Beda 80.38%, UP 76.4%. Bar reforms (Bar Matter 1161, June 2004): five-failure rule, 50% disqualification, multiple choice. Legal education reform failures: four proposals (accreditation, clinical education, sanctions on sub-standard schools, national admission test) were not acted on but referred to the Legal Education Board which, 'although created 14 years ago, has not been operationalized.' CJP closes with his EC legacy: 'The doors to our legal profession must swing on reluctant hinges. Those who want to pass those doors must make a solemn commitment to adhere to an ethical compass. Quality justice always begins with a high standard of ethics... competent and ethical attorneys, code-named EC, that is the legacy I would like to leave our profession.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered on December 6, 2006 at the Supreme Court Session Hall as his retirement valedictory, CJ Panganiban structures his thanksgiving in concentric circles -- first the two Presidents who appointed him (Ramos to the Court on October 10, 1995, and Arroyo as 21st Chief Justice on December 21, 2005), then his Supreme Court colleagues, his teachers from Candaba Elementary to FEU, his spiritual shepherds led by Fr. Michael Nolan and Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, and finally his wife Leni and their five children and nine grandchildren. He uses the occasion to crystallize the institutional vocabulary of what he calls 'the Panganiban Court': the 'Four Ins' the judiciary must embody (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence), the four institutional vices it must resist (influence, interference, indifference, insolence), the 'plague of ships' that corrodes impartiality (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), and the 'ACID problems' that the Action Program for Judicial Reform attacks (limited Access by the poor, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay). All of these, he argues, are means toward the twin end-goals of safeguarding liberty AND nurturing prosperity under the rule of law, exemplified by the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity he convened October 18-20, 2006. He closes with a personal Psalm-23 echoing prayer dedicating his life to God.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 29, 2006 at a two-day Asian constitutional courts conference -- one week before CJP's mandatory retirement -- this address presents the liberty-and-prosperity twin-standard framework to an international judicial audience. CJP opens with a structural clarification: unlike the other countries attending, the Philippines has no separate constitutional court; the SC discharges all constitutional court functions. He presents the historical context (Philippine Bill of Rights zealously guarded; courts as great equalizers against State power) and the constitutional economic rights mandate (just and dynamic social order; equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth). He describes the two standards of review: (1) strict scrutiny for civil and political rights -- 'scales of justice have weighed heavily against government and in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak'; (2) deferential stance for prosperity and development issues -- 'deference is accorded to the political branches of government, namely the Presidency and Congress.' The October 18-20, 2006 Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity provided the governing international evidence: 'unanimity on the need to pursue both liberty and prosperity'; but also the caveat that 'each country must pursue internally its own quest for its own philosophical and jurisprudential identity.' Philippines-specific conclusion: 'the peculiar facts and distinct circumstances of the Philippines make the formula Liberty and Prosperity still the most viable economic and judicial philosophy here. After all, during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.' Closing: 'I wish the Asian constitutional courts good speed and success in finding and striking the right balance between the sometimes contending demands and jurisdictions of the state, culture and religion; and, if I may add, those of safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our peoples.'

Melencio-Herrera ('Justice Amor'); nine days before CJP's mandatory retirement -- this address by CJP opens with the Hukom Juan Suplado (CID) joke: a fictional judge is offered a Mercedes Benz S560 for sale at 1,000 pesos and says 'In that case, I will buy two!' -- illustrating the three complaints against the judiciary: corruption (accepting a bribe), incompetence (failing to see the problem), and delay (managing a case ex-parte). He identifies ACID (access, corruption, incompetence, delay) as 'the special focus of my chief justiceship' and focuses on the 'D': the problem of delay is caused by both systemic factors (the adversarial system's inherent slowness) and man-made factors (litigants and lawyers who misuse and abuse the Rules of Court). The solution: court-annexed mediation as a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial court level; recently approved also at the Court of Appeals level; PhilJA is studying the feasibility of court-annexed arbitration ('less time-consuming, less tedious, less confrontational, and more productive of goodwill and lasting relationships'). Tribute to the mediators: 'Ayusin ang Gusot, Habaan ang Pasensiya; to be successful peacemakers, you must exude professionalism and practice patience. Accept the difficulty of your work and have the persistence to reach for an amicable settlement... it is the knowledge of promoting peace that will bring self-worth and true happiness.' Closing: 'I am convinced that all of you have helped my chief justiceship in addressing the problems plaguing the judiciary, particularly the D in ACID, or the fight against delay in the delivery of quality judgments.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 18, 2006 as the keynote at the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity -- the most internationally comprehensive speech in the corpus, attended by 300+ jurists, lawyers, diplomats and civil society leaders from multiple countries; supported by UNDP, WB, ADB, CIDA, USAID/TAF, ABA and ROLE; WB President Wolfowitz and ADB President Kuroda sent video messages; US SC Justice Kennedy and Judge Wallace participated by video conference; French CJ Canivet and IBA President Pombo Garcia attended in person -- this address by CJP presents Liberty and Prosperity in global historical and theoretical context. He traces the liberty arc (Magna Carta → French Revolution → American Declaration → Filipino nationhood) and cites three Panganiban Court decisions (Senate v. Ermita, Bayan v. Ermita, David v. Arroyo) plus international cases (Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, Rasul v. Bush, Jameel v. Wall Street Journal, Spanish SC detention ruling, French Cour de Cassation). Both are imperative paradigms in society.'). Philippine dual judicial standard: strict scrutiny for liberty; deferential interpretation for prosperity; the 'peculiarly Filipino' grave-abuse-of-discretion exception (tracing to the previous dictatorial regime). The governing political psychology claim: 'our people value their freedoms very dearly and will not exchange them for food. The Filipinos may endure occasional hunger, but they will never tolerate injustice and indignity for long.' He discusses economic development theories (Easterly's Elusive Quest, Bremmer's J Curve, the law-and-finance school) and closes: 'each country has its own history, experience, temperament, economics, culture and politics, which should determine how viable Liberty and Prosperity would be in its jurisdiction,' proposing a possible global foundation for Liberty and Prosperity with international awards.

Comelec ('party-list system is reserved for the poor and the marginalized'). During that global gathering, we hope to spread the gospel of Liberty and Prosperity beyond our shores and unto the world.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered as closing remarks at the FLP Awards Ceremony at Manila Polo Club on September 2, 2024, this speech has two parts. The first thanks the special guests seated around Panganiban's table, organized counterclockwise -- Special Guest First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos (whose birthday is being doubly celebrated since the ceremony was rescheduled from August 19 to a date sacred to her), guest speaker MVP (Manuel V. Pangilinan), CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo (chair of the Law Scholarship Board of Judges), Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando, Lucio 'Hun Hun' Tan III (Tan Yan Kee Foundation), Solomon Hermosura (representing Ayala Corporation), Arthur and Alfred Ty (Metrobank Foundation), former BSP Governor 'Say' Tetangco (SM Investments), and FLP President Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez. The second part lays out Panganiban's foundational thesis: all five Philippine Constitutions are libertarian in their Bills of Rights, but political libertarianism of the mind must be paired with liberation from extreme poverty -- freedom for the spirit AND food for the body, freedom from fear AND freedom from want, under the rule of law, not dictators. one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 3, 2021 as the keynote and induction address at PICPA's national conference, this speech by CJP -- who opens by humorously questioning why Dolly Miguel invited 'not a CPA, not even a commerce or business administration graduate' to be their inducting officer -- makes the case that CPAs, CFOs and CEOs are directly relevant to the philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law through the four TATS values: Transparency, Accountability, Truth and Sustainability. He first establishes the relationship with incoming PICPA President Dolly Miguel through their shared PLDT, MPIC, Meralco and GMA7 experience -- she as SGV partner-in-charge of external audits, he as Audit Committee chairman -- noting the multi-jurisdictional complexity of auditing PLDT (NYSE-listed, HK-listed parent, Philippine regulations) and Dolly's consistent performance under intense grilling. His L&P thesis is anchored in MLK ('If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty nor the possibility for the pursuit of happiness') -- quoted not for his nationality but because 'truth is eternal and limitless; truth is not bound by sovereignty, or territory, or ideology.' He proves the entrepreneurship-prosperity link through three natural experiments: the US (pioneers unleashing Edison, Ford, Gates, Jobs, Bezos, contained by good governance); China (Deng Xiaoping's One-Country-Two-Systems unlocking Jack Ma and others); and the Korea comparison (South's private-initiative prosperity vs. North's poverty from tight grip on freedom). He then argues that different nations can sequence liberty and prosperity differently but must eventually achieve both in equal measure. TATS values, he concludes, make accountants 'images and collaborators of Martin Luther King, of Confucius and his fisherman, of Thomas Edison, of J.P. Morgan, of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, of Steve Jobs and even of Deng Xiaoping and Jack Ma.' He closes with FLP's three first-decade programs (20 law scholarships, dissertation contests, 17 professorial chairs) and announces the second-decade ESMEL expansion -- including a proposed AIM MBA major in Legal Management welcomed by AIM President Jikyeong Kang.

Third, free competition: businesses never rent-seeking, never dependent on political or family connections; transparency via stock market listing; hired people smarter than themselves and paid them well; 'The business is not there to serve the family'; Lance sold Jack and Jill snacks as management trainee in an old Datsun with a broken aircon; Robina started as a bodega clerk; Marcia scooped ice cream -- 'hindi puede ang puede na.' one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 23, 2019 at the book launch of 'Momentum: Economic Reforms for Sustaining Growth' (edited by Roel Landingin, with essays by Romeo Bernardo, Calixto Chikiamco, Emmanuel de Dios, Raul Fabella, and the late Cayetano Paderanga), this speech by CJP opens with the Shakespeare 'kill all lawyers' joke and declares that the book's authors -- 'if ever there would be a Supreme Court for economic matters' -- would easily constitute some of its most revered members. He proposes that his liberty-and-prosperity legal philosophy is in 'legal equilibrium' with the economists' thesis: the same truth reached from law (judicial decisions) and economics (econometric analysis). He then makes the constitutional-architecture diagnosis: the 1987 Philippine Constitution places political rights (Bill of Rights -- mandatory, self-executing, no implementing legislation needed) above prosperity provisions (Declaration of Principles, Social Justice, Education articles -- aspirational, not self-executing, requiring implementing laws), a design born from the centuries-old Filipino struggle against colonial domination (Spain, America) and the Patrick Henry 'give me liberty or give me death' tradition. He presents his most important economic ponencia -- Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997) -- where he had to overcome the reigning 'Filipino First' doctrine, beginning with only 3 full concurrers and eventually convincing all 14 other justices through 'days of patient explanations, discussions and deliberations' to unanimously uphold WTO membership and embrace globalization, liberalization, deregulation and privatization. He then describes the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 18-20, 2006) -- SC-sponsored, funded by the World Bank, USAID, CIDA, EU and Asia Foundation, attended by ~300 international jurists -- where Canadian CJ Beverley McLachlin proposed renaming the philosophy 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law,' and the Manila Declaration was adopted calling for triennial reconvening. He notes with regret that his successors as CJ did not pursue the reconvening and that the Court returned to prioritizing liberty over prosperity. He closes by describing FLP's programs (20 professorial chairs, 20 scholarships, dissertation contest) and announcing plans for a roving Museum on Liberty and Prosperity in 2020 and a Global Forum reconvening in 2021.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 16, 2019 to the Good Governance Advocates and Practitioners of the Philippines (GGAPP) at SM Aura, this speech by CJP -- opened with the Jolly Restaurant aging-forgetfulness joke (group of men who at 80 agree to meet there because they had never been there before) -- recounts 12+ years of corporate directorship experience. The centerpiece is the 2008 Meralco corporate coup: called from New York by Chairman Manolo Lopez while tending to newborn grandson Matthew, CJP flew back in time for the May 27, 2008 shareholders meeting where an ex-parte SEC restraining order was read to block the Lopez Group's proxies. Advising patriarch Oscar Lopez privately that the order was 'invalid and gravely abusive' and that obeying it would allow a 42% minority coalition to control the company, CJP recommended proceeding with the election -- the manual ballot count ran till midnight, the longest in corporate memory, and the SEC order was later judicially voided. He also narrates his Hernandez v. Napocor intervention (convening Dasmarinas Village complainants at his home to find a win-win solution that resulted in their desisting from executing the SC's own final order once WHO and international experts found no conclusive cancer-radiation link), the Petron entry (Ramon Ang's last-day offer after observing CJP: 'I thought you only knew law -- I now know you also know business pala'; permission sought from and given by Pangilinan: 'I fully trust you and I know you will not reveal our secrets'), the PLDT NYSE investigation (CJP's independent voluminous report exonerating top officials, staking his career and reputation on it; investors never filed), and the Jollibee NED (SEC rejected him as ID; Tony Tan Caktiong nominated him as NED instead -- 'my rejection as an ID was a blessing in disguise'). He articulates the ID's main duty -- fidelity to the corporation, not loyalty to any shareholder -- and his four criteria: culture fit, no contentious rivalry, substantive preparation, and strict time management. He closes: 'retirement merely meant a change of tires to embark on a new independent journey in the business world.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered at the first-night wake of Dr. George S.K. Ty on November 24, 2018 -- the night after his death -- this eulogy by CJP was prepared under extraordinary circumstances: Nick Torres called CJP while he was seated beside President Duterte at the San Beda function; CJP texted Cardinal Tagle (in Hong Kong) mid-event; Tagle flew back and celebrated the Mass; CJP skipped the FEU Law Alumni Diamond Jubilee Tamaraw Award (given only once every 50 years) to attend, sending daughter Tet in his stead. He structures the eulogy as nine personal stories, each illuminating a character virtue. Story 1: as Board of Judges chair for Metrobank's Outstanding Teachers search, CJP observed Dr. Ty's soft smile when he asked a teacher why Metrobank would reward her when she gave the bank nothing in return; their friendship 'flourished purely on mutual respect and genuine brotherly affection. He never asked from, or was given any favor by, me as a sitting member of the Supreme Court.' Story 3: CJP praised Alfred's golf game to Dr. Ty at a GT Tower lunch; Dr. Ty summoned Alfred and told him that being a very good golfer was 'bad' -- it meant too much time on the course; 'Since then, I stopped playing with him, lest I slipped and put him in trouble again.' Story 4: Jaime Zobel invited CJP to BPI; Dr. Ty's immediate response by phone: 'Please accept. I fully trust you. I know you will never reveal any business secret.' Story 5: CJP asked if the FLP could buy a used Toyota Innova at APEC discount prices; a week later, Dr. Ty arrived with a brand-new red Innova already registered in FLP's name. Story 6: Dr. Ty pledged 10% of his total wealth to philanthropy (vs. the corporate 2% of net income standard); donated P1 billion for the Toyota Institute of Technology; at a private dinner for retired Toyota Japan Chairman Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda -- who explained that Toyota yielded Philippine majority control because it was the only market where Toyota topped all brands for 27 consecutive years, not even equaled in Japan -- Toyoda was so impressed he matched the P1 billion, doubling the total for students. Story 7: Dr. Ty built the Mary the Queen Catholic Church in Nanjing single-handedly; CJP leveraged this act of faith to approach him for the Manila Cathedral restoration, making him one of its largest donors. The eulogy closes with John 14:1-4 and a 12-virtue inventory -- integrity, industry, fairness, generosity, honor, dignity, meekness, thoughtfulness, trustworthiness, discipline and dedication to duty -- as the legacy to be personified by those left behind.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 17, 2018 in Cebu as a closing response to PALS President Dean Joan S. Largo's lecture on constitutional provisions for social justice and human rights, this speech by CJP takes a complementary rather than contesting stance: Dean Largo focused on enforcing social justice provisions via judicial remedies (citing South Africa, Argentina and Colombia) -- on dole-outs, conditional cash transfers, cheap rice, communal housing; CJP's response moves one level deeper to the structural solution. He cites Martin Luther King's 'If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty' -- deployed 'not because of his nationality, color, gender or religion' but because 'truth is eternal and transcends sovereignty.' He advances the twin beacons thesis ('humans need both justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; liberty and prosperity -- these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other') and grounds it in Confucius' fisherman parable, arguing that the goal of governance is not dole-outs but teaching, assisting with tools, providing freedom, and enabling entrepreneurial genius. He validates the thesis across three natural experiments: the US (Edison, Tesla, Ford, Gates, Jobs, contained by FDR/Eisenhower/Obama good governance), China (Deng Xiaoping's One-Country-Two-Systems unleashing Jack Ma's generation), and the Korea comparison (South Korea's private initiative vs. North Korea's 'abject poverty as a result of its tight grip on creativity'). His specifically Filipino proof: OFW engineers, nurses and doctors 'earn more than the average Caucasians' in the US, Canada and Australia and 'observe strict traffic rules simply because these rules are enforced evenly and fairly' -- demonstrating that the problem is governance, not the Filipino character. He notes FLP's programs in Cebu (13 professorial chairs, 20 law scholarships, USC student Tess Marie Tan winning 2nd in the Dissertation Contest) and closes: 'if our Filipino brethren are accorded liberty, prosperity and the rule of law, they will use their entrepreneurial ingenuity to uplift themselves from destitution, disease and disability.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered February 26, 2015 as the opening luncheon address at the 12th ALA General Assembly -- on the theme 'Sharing Prosperity at the Crossroads of ASEAN Integration: the Legal Challenges,' at the invitation of incoming ALA President Ave Cruz -- this speech by CJP opens by twice quoting Martin Luther King: 'If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty nor the possibility for the pursuit of happiness.' He grounds the ALA theme in his twin beacons philosophy ('justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; liberty and prosperity -- one is useless without the other') and in FLP's founding mission (2011, CJP's 75th birthday). He advances the Confucius fisherman thesis with its governance corollary: government provides guarantees, incentives, institutions and minimal regulations -- not to give fish but to teach fishing, fund the boat, allow ocean access, and teach marketing. Three natural experiments validate the thesis: the US (Edison through Jobs, contained by FDR/Eisenhower good governance); China (Deng Xiaoping's One-Country-Two-Systems unleashing entrepreneurial ingenuity); and the Korea comparison (South Korea's private initiative vs. North Korea's 'abject poverty as a result of its tight grip on creativity'). He identifies the ASEAN rising stars: Singapore (first world), Malaysia and Thailand (exemplars), and 'the VIPs of the world, Vietnam, Indonesia and Philippines' with enviable GDP growth records. The speech's most concrete policy recommendation: the Philippines' 34-day, 16-step, 17%-of-per-capita-income process to start a business vs. Malaysia's 6-day, 3-step, 7% -- 'certainly, the lawyers of Asean can easily help solve this simple problem by tapping Malaysia as the model.' He closes with optimism: at the Assembly's opening he sees happy faces; at the closing, he expects 'even happier faces for, by then, we would have accomplished our mission.'

His dual standard from Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters; private enterprise as the engine; the economic pie must be enlarged and fairly divided. He analyzes recent SC decisions: Belgica reversed LAMP on PDAF; MOA-AD got a TRO (no transparency) but FAB did not (transparent process); EDCA unchallenged; Gamboa v. Teves should be applied prospectively. The constitutional interpretation debate: he personally visited Justice Scalia to invite him to the Global Forum; Scalia declined ('I do not believe in international law'); Justice Kennedy agreed to speak via teleconference. one_paragraph_summary: Delivered February 23, 2014 as the guest speaker at the Mapa High School Grand Alumni Homecoming at Metro Tent, Ortigas Center -- the most comprehensive single-speech autobiography in the corpus -- this address by CJP to Congressman Benny Abante Jr. (MHSAA President), Desidero Gurno (VMapa Foundation), and Leonides Bernabe Sr. (Blue Falcon Association) opens with the institutional memory of Mapa High: one of four Manila public high schools named after deceased jurists (Arellano, Araullo, Mapa, Torres), the largest with 6,000+ students, starting CJP from the Guipit Annex (where they squatted on cement floors for lack of desks) through to the main building. Four teachers are named: Mrs. Rocio Kapunan (economics; required savings bank accounts), Ms. Leticia Ramirez (English grammar 'I used when I wrote my decisions in the Supreme Court'), Mrs. Magdalena Aytona (social studies), and Ms. Gloria Reyes (Tagalog). CJP then recounts his full life arc: from hawking newspapers at age eight, sleeping on cold sidewalks, promising himself to be president of the Manila Times; through the UP 15-centavo barrier and the UST Trinity failure ('Susmaryosep! Jesus, Maria at Joseph'); to FEU (Salonga, Roces, Evangelista, Fr. Nolan); to selling textbooks and bibles in college; to the 1960 bar exams (cum laude, sick, flooded, 6th place); to Baron Travel Corporation (funded all five children's US graduate studies -- Harvard, Stanford, UC, Chicago, Michigan); to ASTA chairmanship (first Asian and only Filipino international chairman, Rome 1985); to the 1991 Inquirer presidency (the newsboy dream fulfilled); to the Tagalog SC offer exchange with Ramos ('Ah, sa Supreme Court ka na lang'; CJP: 'Huwag po sana ninyong i-lalang ang Supreme Court') and GMA's appointment without prior interview; to the Lambino v. Comelec 8-7 victory in 2006 that preserved the presidential system; to retirement (new tires, independent directors, Inquirer column despite Salonga's 'Chief justices do not write history; they make history' warning). Three foundations now: Metrobank Foundation Board of Advisers chair, Manila Cathedral Foundation President, FLP Board of Trustees chair. Giving back: half of SC retirement pay to FLP; one year's Inquirer column income to the Inquirer Foundation for Newsboys; today, eight subsistence scholarships for poor but deserving Mapans. He closes with the governing thesis: 'poverty is not an excuse for failure -- it became our challenge for our success'; the three Ts (time, talent, treasure); 'no one is so poor he cannot share something; and no one is so rich he does not need anything'; and the 1995 prayer: 'The Lord is my Shepherd. He has given me more than I deserve... an opportunity to be remembered longer than my own life.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 29, 2012 at Manila Golf Club for ACCRA Law's 40th Anniversary BusinessLaw Forum jointly with the Management Association of the Philippines, Panganiban uses three of his own landmark ponencias to lay out his settled jurisprudential philosophy of 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law' -- a phrase he credits to Canada's CJ Beverley McLachlin after the 2006 Global Forum. His two-track theory: in political/civil-liberty cases the scales weigh heavily against the government via strict scrutiny; in economic/policy cases courts must defer to the Executive and Congress unless there is grave abuse of discretion or blatant constitutional violation. He demonstrates this with (1) Tanada vs Angara (1997), the unanimous decision he authored upholding the Senate's WTO Treaty ratification by holding that the Constitution balances bias-for-Filipino-goods against business reciprocity, and that the 'wisdom or viability' of globalization is outside judicial review; (2) La Bugal-B'laan vs Ramos (Dec 1, 2004 MR 10-4 reversing the Jan 27, 2004 original 8-5 ruling), where he authored the reconsideration upholding the Mining Law, the IRR, and the FTAA on the principle that the Constitution must be read 'in broad, life-giving strokes' rather than to 'strangulate economic growth'; and (3) Gamboa vs Teves (June 28, 2011), where he diplomatically critiques the SC majority for departing from deferential interpretation by reading 'capital' in Art XII Sec 11 to mean only voting common shares -- siding implicitly with the dissenters who argued the 1935 framers' intent covered all shares. He notes that 2012 Philippine GDP growth (6.3%/5.9%/7.1% across Q1/Q2/Q3, best in ASEAN, second in Asia after China) shows the country's economic momentum is real and worth protecting -- and closes by reiterating that the recognized engine of growth in a free enterprise regime is the private sector, to which the judiciary should defer.

He applies Donaldson's lessons to Philippine realities: the 2008 Lehman Brothers/AIG collapse mirrors local pyramiding scams vowing '50 percent rewards monthly' ('when something is too good to be true, it is indeed never good and never true'); the parable of the shadu (pointing fingers at failures) and the knee-jerk legislative response are both wrong -- 'too many regulations penalize the law-abiding; laws tend to punish past wrongdoings but rarely address future witchcraft of the unethical because lawbreakers simply invent new ways to steal.' Donaldson's concept of 'paying for peril' (borrowing short on fluctuating rates, lending long on fixed rates) explains why such entities 'will never stabilize and will always be at risk.' He closes with personal thanks to Manuel V. Pangilinan for 'giving me the opportunity to be an independent director in some of the leading companies of this conglomerate; as a retired jurist used to working in an environment of independence and integrity, I have found fulfillment and contentment in the high standards of ethics and corporate governance that characterize our undertakings in the First Pacific Group.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 28, 2011 at the Institute of Corporate Directors Breakfast Roundtable -- invited by Chairman Dr. Jesus P. Estanislao -- this six-topic address by CJP analyzes the nature, duties, independence safeguards, SEC propositions and remedies for Independent Directors. An ID must own at least one share, be elected per the Corporation Code, serve as a trustee/fiduciary of the corporation above private interests, and receive no additional compensation beyond director fees. SRC Section 38 defines IDs through negative covenants ('other than an officer or employee... having a relationship... which would interfere with independent judgment') -- 'worded like the Ten Commandments.' The ID's distinctive duty: fiscalize and counter-check management and controlling shareholders; uphold laws, articles, bylaws, ethics canons and governance manuals; be 'sufficiently courageous and independent' to oppose management when necessary. Unlike judges, IDs have no constitutional security of tenure or compensation -- their continuation depends on controlling shareholders. On the SEC's proposed 5-5 plan (five consecutive years per corporation; maximum five PLCs simultaneously): 'like the Ten Commandments and the SRC, these prohibitions are NOT provided in the SRC but are SEC-originated inventions and impositions.' The SC justice analogy: 'Can SC justices appointed annually by the President and whose compensation depends totally on Congress be expected to be independent? By the same token, can we truly expect full independence from IDs who depend on the votes of the majority?' The solution: 'instead of restricting the prerogatives of IDs, the first order of the day should be to strengthen their independence and integrity so they can perform their lonely work effectively.' Four remedies: persuasion, administrative route, judicial route (showing SEC exceeded its authority), and Ombudsman complaints against SEC officials. Close: 'the end never justifies the means. However laudable its motives, the SEC must not impose unreasonable, whimsical and illegal inventions beyond its legal mandate.'

Excellence is the governing Foundation philosophy: 'it seeks, aspires for, bathes in and promotes excellence all the time, everywhere... God has given each of us, without exception, a natural talent. It is everyone's responsibility to discover and to develop to the maximum whatever natural gift the Lord has endowed us.' Let us not be frustrated, let us not give up... let us persevere.' The 30th Anniversary theme is Excel, Engage, Empower (three Es); 'the beacon and the anchor is the first: EXCEL'; but 'the three Es must be accompanied by the one T that our group chairman is known for, and that is TRUST. EXCELLENCE and TRUST must go together because they mutually reinforce each other. We celebrate Metrobank Foundation's three Es, as in Excel, Engage, Empower, because they are backed up by one T as in George S.K. Ty.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 22, 2008 on behalf of Lopez Group board members and officials at the two-day seminar 'Living Excellence and Social Responsibility the Lopez Way,' this address by CJP -- as an independent director of First Philippine Holdings and Meralco -- analyzes the Lopez Group's twin commitments. The Lopez Group is 'one of the most storied business families in Philippine history'; patriarch Don Eugenio Lopez Sr. built an empire spanning energy, media and real estate; 'the Lopez family has demonstrated that private enterprise and public responsibility can and must go together.' Excellence: 'doing everything we do at the highest possible standard... striving for quality in every product, every service, every decision.' But 'excellence without social responsibility becomes mere profit-seeking at the expense of the community.' Social responsibility means serving employees, customers, communities and country -- the Lopez Group fulfills this through energy investments that 'serve the basic needs of millions of Filipinos' and media properties that 'serve the democratic ideals of free expression and access to information.' The liberty-and-prosperity connection: 'businesses that operate with integrity, that pay their taxes, that respect their workers' rights, that tell the truth in their public communications, are not just good corporate citizens. They are pillars of a democratic society.' Conversely, 'businesses that evade taxes, that exploit their workers, that engage in corruption and bribery, undermine not just their own long-term interests but the fabric of our democratic institutions. The rule of law cannot survive if the powerful systematically circumvent it.' CJP's insider assessment: 'the Lopez Group is genuinely committed to the principles it espouses. It is not perfect, no organization is, but it strives in good faith to live up to its stated values.' He closes by challenging attendees to be 'not just a profitable conglomerate but a principled one, worthy of the trust of the Filipino people.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered at Bert Lina's funeral Mass on Ash Wednesday, March 5, 2025, this eulogy by CJP opens by asking mourners to smile like Bert -- whose portrait reflects his characteristically happy disposition -- and frames death as the beginning of eternal life. The organizing thesis is a three-part love: first, love for family, especially for Sylvia whose extraordinary birthday gifts ranged from a Jaguar car and a Bösendorfer piano to a specially bred pink gumamela variety from UPLB and the Sylvia P. Lina Theater at De La Salle Zobel; his four daughters (April Rose, Donna May, Lucia Jane/Sheila, Bertha Ann) and four grandchildren. Second, love for work -- 21 companies, 2,800 employees treated as 'partners and collaborators, not alalays,' each receiving a free daily healthy meal and production bonuses and profit sharing regardless of rank, fueled by the 'back haul' system and a philosophy that problems are opportunities not obstacles. He served twice as Customs Commissioner (under Arroyo and Aquino III, against CJP's advice) and funded the Manila Symphony Orchestra. Third, love for God -- crediting the Lord with everything, donating Carillons to five churches (Manila Cathedral, St. James Alabang, Naga City, Pila Laguna, Mandaue Cebu) as reminders of mortality, and conducting annual medical-surgical-dental missions. CJP traces the relationship to 1969 when Bert was a junior auditor at L.C. Diaz, became his and Sylvia's wedding sponsor, and considers Donna May his 'daughter by choice.' The climactic one-word reveal -- LOVE, his 'enormous, googolplex love' -- ties all three themes together, closing with 'To God be the glory.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered at a Eucharistic celebration at the Manila Cathedral on September 18, 2024, this award acceptance speech for the Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice -- the highest honor the Holy Father grants lay persons -- opens with CJP declaring himself 'unworthy and undeserving' but acknowledging the award's two grounds: his presidency of the Manila Cathedral Basilica Foundation and his spiritual journey as 'a frail servant.' Citing Matthew 6:1, he accepts because the Vicar of Christ initiated the recognition. The first half pays tribute to all co-workers on the Cathedral's four Rs (retrofit, restrengthen, restore, renovate): five major donor families -- Ramon Ang and Cecil; the late Dr. George S.K. Ty (represented by Arthur/Zandra, Alfred/Cherry, Alessandra/Alvin); Fernando Zobel de Ayala (Jaime Augusto was in Singapore); Alberto and Sylvia Lina (who donated 23 Dutch computerized Carillon Bells to replace the 17-ton belfry bells); and one anonymous donor. DM Consunji donated their mark-ups and margins. He narrates the engineering miracle: no 'as-built' plan existed anywhere; workers dug under the belly, discovered pyramid-like pilings, chipped the marble columns, wrapped them in carbon fiber and injected epoxy -- and restored every marble cover without a single breakage. Cardinal Tagle's text from Rome recalls closing the Cathedral with a torn heart, but 'God was preparing us, and the Cathedral warmly welcomed Pope Francis in 2015.' The second half acknowledges spiritual rescuers: Fr. Michael Nolan (FEU chaplain who taught the three basic prayers and snatched CJP from Marxism, leading to the NUSP); late Leni (two conditions for marriage -- abandon political aspirations; understand her difficult vocation); Ambassador Tita de Villa (led CJP into Catholic lay leadership); and Tessie Sy Coson -- former student who became mentor, admirable 'not because of, but in spite of' being BDO chair. He closes by rededicating the 1995 Cuneta Astrodome vow: 'I dedicate all that I am, and all that I will ever be, to Him who is the Source of everything' -- inviting the congregation to rise and proclaim 'To God Be the Glory.'

one_paragraph_summary: This is the formal introduction of CJP as guest speaker and inducting officer at the PICPA induction ceremony on July 3, 2021, delivered by Dr. Alcala. It opens with 'Ageless Passion' -- a musical tribute composed by National Artist Ryan Cayabyab with lyrics by Kristian Jeff Agustin -- as the thematic hook. The introduction traces his life from newsboy in post-war Manila to his 11-year Supreme Court stint, recounts the December 6, 2006 unanimous resolution acclaiming him '21st Century's Renaissance Jurist,' the April 26, 2007 Philippine Bar Association Award of Honor, and Judge Raul Pangalangan's (ICC The Hague) assessment that he 'strove to have as much unanimity as possible' because 'the least dangerous branch speaks loudest when it judges wisely and in one voice.' It enumerates his post-retirement directorial roles (Meralco, Petron, PLDT, Metro Pacific, JG Summit, GMA Network, Jollibee, Metrobank, etc.) and civic leadership (FLP Chairman, Metrobank Foundation, Manila Cathedral Foundation, Permanent Court of Arbitration Philippine Chair, Pontifical Council for the Laity -- only Filipino appointee by Pope John Paul II for 1996-2001). Academic highlights include 6th place in the 1960 Bar at 89.55, FEU Outstanding Alumnus, honorary doctorates from five universities, and 'With Due Respect' ranking 3rd on Amazon's courts bestseller list (behind Jeffrey Toobin and Justice Antonin Scalia). The introduction closes with CJP's family: wife Elenita C. Panganiban and five children (Maria Elena-Yaptangco, Jose Artemio III, Maria Jocelyn-Hannett, Maria Theresa-Manalac, Maria Evelyn-Reagan).

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered at a family gathering on June 5, 2024, this speech by CJP celebrates the simultaneous receipt of masteral scholarships by three grandchildren -- Andrea P. Manalac (University of Michigan MBA, following her mother Tet's footsteps), Rafa P. Yaptangco (Fordham University MBA dean's scholarship, a Jesuit institution to the delight of Ateneo's Fr. Bobby Yap), and Victoria P. Hannett (University of Pennsylvania Master of Biotechnology, chosen from offers at seven programs across six schools including Georgetown x2, Brown, NYU, and American University -- 'champagne problems'). CJP says the news gave him the same elevation as when he was named Chief Justice. He profiles each alphabetically: Andrea the Disney-obsessed singer (36 of 47 Disney World attractions in one day, Hamilton five times in three countries, Taylor Swift in Tokyo twice, Shopee then PwC); Rafa the quiet-but-competitive tech-golfer (caricatures on Lolo's bedroom wall, tonsilitis-driven computer romance as 'competitive advantage,' handicap 30 → single digits in four years, Lazada → TikTok → Fordham); and Victoria the math-science-dance prodigy from Greenwich CT (Georgetown neurobiology, focused on dementia, stroke, and migraine drug discovery, promising to cure dementia by the time CJP turns 92). The governing message -- 'No pain, no gain. No sacrifice, no victory' -- is delivered through a four-witness canon: CJP's own newsboy-shoeshine-house-builder story; Jensen Huang's (Nvidia, $100B+) Stanford speech on pain and suffering; Lance Gokongwei's Jack-and-Jill sari-sari-store management trainee beginnings before inheriting the JG Summit conglomerate; and Jesus Christ's command to take up the cross. The theological upgrade: 'when suffering is undergone with love, it becomes sacrifice.' CJP playfully attributes the scholars' academic genes to their maternal line (Len, Celine, Tet, and Lola Leni -- AIM MBA with honors on a Central Bank full scholarship) rather than to himself ('no elite Philippine school, no graduate degree, no US education, nada'), and closes by invoking Leni's blessing from heaven.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 16, 2023 at the Rotary Club of Manila, this speech by CJP responds to DGE Jackie Rodriguez's invitation to 'show our new members a wonderful glimpse of our glorious past' by reminiscing his 1990-1991 RCM presidency. He opens with a Shakespeare riff ('I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him -- but I have been subpoenaed to be buried instead') and jokes he intends to reach 100 ('only the good die young'). He first narrates how he got to the Supreme Court via a Rotary friendship: when he was inducted in 1983, his RCM seatmate was then-Philippine Constabulary chief Gen. Fidel V. Ramos; on June 17, 1992, FVR called CJP for a one-on-one meeting and offered him Secretary of Justice; CJP declined (he voted for Salonga, not FVR); FVR replied he wanted to 'be president of all our people' and cited CJP's RCM success as proof of trustworthiness; after CJP later cited Leni's objection, FVR uttered the famous line: 'Ah, under the saya ka pala. Dalawa na tayo. Sa Supreme Court ka na lang.' He then details his RCM presidency: 455-member club (largest in the world outside the US); his discernment with BLD members who were 'struck' by Isaiah 42 ('I have called you for the victory of justice... a light for the nations'); the 'Love God Serve Man' credo derived from Mark 12:29-32; a 76-page Program of Action with 178 projects and a P90-million budget (18 times the prior record of P5 million); member outcry and his Matthew 5:11-12 consolation ('Blessed are you when they insult you'). Four days after his July 12, 1990 inaugural, the 7.7-Richter Luzon earthquake struck (2,000+ deaths); three days later at an RCM meeting, CJP pleaded for assistance and members pledged P5.5 million in 30 minutes (plus P660,000 the next day), for a total of nearly P7 million -- 16 times his best expectation of P500,000. Relief operations included a 250-family tent city in Burnham Park, Baguio, and the Rotary Club of Waikiki air-freighting 3,300 kilos from Hawaii. His valedictory reported 185 projects implemented (7 more than planned), 95% completion, 72 committees, and a 94-page Final Report. He closes with the self-description as 'the only Philippine Rotary President to become Chief Justice of the Philippines' and with a sinner's prayer of surrender.
