one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 21, 2023 at the Grand Ballroom of Shangri-La at the Fort for ACCRALAW's 50th Anniversary Gala, this keynote message by CJP opens with the Spanish salutation 'Compañeros y Compañeras, Damas y Caballeros' and thanks Managing Partner Trina Prodigalidad for the invitation. He recalls his 2012 ACCRA 40th anniversary speech on 'How the Judiciary Can Help the Economy' (covering Tanada v. Angara, La Bugal B'laan v. Ramos, and Gamboa v. Teves). He aligns ACCRA's 'Beyond Legal Excellence' CSR theme with FLP's philosophy -- citing Confucius ('teach a man to fish') as the governing principle -- and invites ACCRA to partner with FLP on the Museum for Liberty and Prosperity and the Prosperity Fund. He confesses his deepest professional regret: not joining ACCRA at its inception (he had too many prior commitments -- all of which became ACCRA clients anyway). Prodigalidad,' guest of honor at ACCRA's 2048 diamond anniversary. He notes that none of the founders ever intruded in his Court work, and that he has 'invariably recommended ACCRA' since retirement. one_paragraph_summary: Published April 9, 2023 -- the day of her passing -- this memorial biography of Professor Elenita 'Leni' Carpio-Panganiban, CJP's wife of 62 years, is structured in four sections: loving wife, nurturing mother, inspiring professor and colleague, and faithful daughter of God. Born on the leap-year date of February 29, 1940, she graduated cum laude from St. Scholastica's College, earned an MA in Statistics from UP's Statistical Center, and completed her MBA at AIM in 1971 as one of four women in the pioneering batch -- on a Central Bank full scholarship after 13 years as statistician and economist. She joined AIM's faculty in 1973 as its first woman faculty member and taught for 37 years (retiring 2009), serving as MBM Coordinator multiple terms and Associate Dean 1999-2000; her daughter Tet is now also an AIM professor. Msgr. Gerry Santos narrated their meeting: a 1958 train to Naga City for an NUSP Seminar on Communism (Art was NUSP president, Leni represented St. Scholastica's; she had wanted to be a Benedictine nun). They married April 8, 1961 at Immaculate Conception Parish Church in Cubao. The 2021 Diamond Anniversary was held privately at Carmelite Chapel, Tagaytay, presided by Cardinal Advincula and attended by all 86 incumbent Philippine archbishops and bishops. The couple returned from a joyful Singapore trip on April 7, 2023, privately celebrated their 62nd anniversary on April 8, and Leni passed suddenly on April 9 -- 'That is so Mom, giving us a gift to the very end' (Archie's eulogy). The biography quotes all five children: Celine ('My Mom was my image of perfection'); Len ('She was a constant, reassuring presence'); Archie (the April 8 phone call found her 'very happy and talkative... less than 24 hours later, she was gone'); Tet (Leni's letter: 'Tet, you are so quiet... You have to learn to fight'); and Mabel ('Mom put family above all else'). CJP calls her 'the gentle wind beneath my wings and the inspiration of my humble career.'

Advincula marking the Panganiban Diamond Wedding (61st) Anniversary in coincidence with the CBCP Annual Plenary Assembly, this is Panganiban's most extended spiritual autobiography. Michael Nolan and Dean Jovito Salonga; courting Leni Carpio (NUS counterpart from St. Scholastica's) whose 'magical Yes' required monthly confession and Sunday Mass at Cubao Immaculate Conception; St. Scholastica Sisters and Fr. Anselmo Bustos disapproving because Leni was novitiate-bound; wedding on April 8, 1961; 1986 Marriage Encounter (cerebral) and Life in the Spirit Seminar (LSS -- 'soul-piercing,' vision of risen Christ, 'spiritual tongues of fire'); catechism with Monsignor Gerry Santos; reading 100+ Christian books including Barclay's 16-volume Daily Study Bible; Ninang Tita de Villa drawing him into the Council of the Laity, PCP-II (1991), PPCRV, the Pontifical Council for the Laity in the Vatican (1996-2002 -- the only Filipino + only incumbent SC justice so appointed), and the Manila Cathedral retrofitting foundation. Ramos offered him Justice Secretary in June 1992; CBCP was split (Archbishop Legaspi urging decline, Bishop Bacani urging accept); Leni broke the tie with her veto on politicians' wives; Ramos responded 'Under the saya ka pala... Dalawa na tayo' and redirected him to the SC. The most quoted anecdote: in January 2006 he told then-Sandiganbayan-nominee Alex Gesmundo to 'sit on my chair because one day you will be sitting there anyway as chief justice' -- a prophecy fulfilled and recounted with Gesmundo present at the anniversary.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 28, 2022 as the commencement address to 250 FEU-NRMF graduates, this speech by CJP -- who acknowledges he normally declines speaking invitations at age 85 but could not refuse his compadre and 60-year friend President Antonio Abad Jr. -- is built around two pieces of advice: always pray and trust God, and work with competence and care. The first is illustrated by a cumulative near-death inventory: dysentery at age 6 in wartime Candaba, Pampanga (no hospital, no medicine, given up for dead, revived in his mother's arms); a severe stomach ache touring Mayon Volcano in 1958 misdiagnosed as indigestion at a maternity clinic (treated with castor oil and morphine, slept 24 hours, woke up pain-free and attended the dance party); two weeks later, the same pain recurred at FEU law school and he was rushed to FEU Hospital where Dr. Ricardo Alfonso -- knowing CJP as the vocal opponent of the compulsory P6 medical fee -- offered him a choice between full billing and the six-peso fee; CJP surrendered: 'Doctor, you win. I will withdraw my opposition.' Surgery revealed a ruptured appendix, unusually at the rear left, contained by fat; he also survived being run over by a six-by-six truck in 1949 as a nine-year-old newspaper peddler on España Street, whose clearance was just enough for his 'lean and thin body to slide under its axles.' He attributes all escapes to divine providence (Isaiah 55:8-10: 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, my ways are not your ways') and traces his own prayer life to FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan's four basic prayers -- including the FEU Prayer that became the basis of the Centennial Prayer of the Courts (2001, still recited in all courts today). The second advice, care, is illustrated by two contrasting witnesses: an unnamed Filipino billionaire who regretted his Houston heart-bypass hospitalization where American doctors treated him as 'an object to be studied' rather than 'a human being with emotions of fear, loneliness and desperation'; and Dr. Horatio 'Cabby' Cabasares, who served Perry, Georgia (pop. 19,000) with Filipino caring and empathy from 1973 until his COVID-19 death on December 16, 2020, honored with a bronze plaque. CJP closes: 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 7, 2021 -- CJP's 85th birthday -- at the Philippine Daily Inquirer for the book launch of 'With Due Respect 3' (WDR3), this speech opens with CJP expressing being 'overwhelmed with honor and joy' that Marixi Rufino Prieto and her daughter Sandy Prieto-Romualdez 'perpetualize my humble work into books every five years' -- the third volume in the series (WDR1: 2011, WDR2: 2016, WDR3: December 7, 2021), this time in two volumes. He narrates the origin story: he was deeply hesitant to accept Marixi's invitation to write for the Inquirer, having witnessed firsthand the rigors of column-writing as lawyer to famous columnist Teodoro Valencia, and having never written a column in his life. When he told Marixi of Salonga's warning -- 'Chief justices make history. They do not write it' -- she countered: 'Dr. Salonga may be correct, but I do not know of any retired chief justice who had been offered to write a column.' A compromise was struck: once weekly instead of the proposed thrice. He has written every Sunday without fail for 15 years (February 2007 to December 2021), despite illness, five annual foreign trips, and directorial duties in 15+ companies and foundations. He credits Marixi for the Amazon achievement: WDR1 ranked 3rd on the courts bestseller list behind Jeffrey Toobin (1st) and the late Justice Antonin Scalia (2nd). He discloses that he was sued for libel over his November 7, 2021 'Disini to pay damages in BNPP suit' column -- but was absolutely cleared by the DOJ and the CA. He thanks CJ Gesmundo for launching the book -- a particularly meaningful gesture since CJP intuited in January 2006 (when Gesmundo came to his Chamber to be sworn in as Sandiganbayan justice) that he should sit on the Chief Justice's chair: 'Please sit on my chair because one day you will be sitting there anyway as chief justice. I must have been led by the Holy Spirit.' He thanks Sean James Borja -- Ateneo valedictorian, 2018 bar topnotcher, and FLP's first scholar-bar-sitter -- for arranging WDR3 topically rather than chronologically, JV Rufino (Inquirer Books), and the editorial team, closing with: 'May they never tire of teaching this aging jurist the rudiments of the English language.'

one_paragraph_summary: Published December 7, 2021 on cjpanganiban.com as a companion to SC025, these are CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo's remarks at the book launch of 'With Due Respect 3' on CJP's 85th birthday. Gesmundo opens with a personal disclosure: when the JBC asked during his CJ interview whether justices' terms should extend beyond 70 (like US lifetime tenure), he immediately said no -- 'at a certain point in life, the productivity of a person wanes.' Looking at CJP at 85, he admits: 'I may have spoken too soon.' He then deploys CJP's example as a paradoxical proof: CJP is 'proving to be the best argument to a lifetime tenure for Justices' -- yet Gesmundo uses this as an argument for fixed retirement, not against it, because 'one can be more prolific and more productive even outside the Court,' and fixed tenure assures institutional renewal through 'a continuous stream of justices.' He presents a concise biographical sketch: self-made man, FEU, 6th in 1960 bar, Salonga-mentored, multi-dimensional career, over 1,000 ponencias, and 15 years of post-retirement relevance. He identifies CJP's 'most influential and potent tool for remaining relevant' as the WDR column -- which discusses burning legal issues 'with more freedom than he had when sitting in the Court... articulating sentiments and views which incumbent members of the Court could only wish to say themselves.' He articulates his own reform agenda -- efficiency, innovation and access on the guiding principles of timely-and-fair, transparent-and-accountable, equal-and-inclusive, adaptive management -- and invites CJP's column as a 'potent aid' in championing it. He responds to CJP's October 31, 2021 confession of not having done enough: 'The work is never finished.' He closes by suggesting CJP's next book title: 'The Art of Relevance,' and thanking him as 'our unofficial resident amicus curiae.'

one_paragraph_summary: Published September 20, 2020, this spiritual memoir by CJP narrates how he and Leni attended 'Marriage Encounter Class 26' at Mirador Villa, Baguio in May 1986 -- invited by a couple-friend who knew of their 'mid-life marital problems' -- and how the weekend transformed them from a divided couple to 'a united whole that completely surrendered all cares and pains to our Lord.' The journey itself began with a double flat tire: the car blew a tire en route from Quezon City; the spare also went flat; they were stranded in Tarlac for over an hour. When they arrived apologizing, their hosts congratulated them: 'the evil one usually visits couples going to Mirador with similar problems to discourage them from going farther.' ME Class 26 featured about 15 couples welcomed by BLD's Praise Ministry; a small room with shared facilities; a 24-hour Adoration chapel tended by the Intercessory Ministry; and the 'auxiliaries' -- prominent professionals and government figures from a previous ME class who served as cooks, waiters, ushers and prayer warriors. The ME format was not classroom lectures but the 'sharing of experiences' of two couples (one with benign problems, one who had separated before finding Christ), followed by the homily of Fr. Pascual Adorable SJ -- the 'Lightning Rod of God' -- whose words 'penetrated deep into our body, soul and spirit.' Three weeks later, CJP and Leni returned to Mirador as volunteer sponsor-couples for the next batch, 'singing to them, serving them and praying for them, and sharing our own transformation in Christ.' The central disclosure of the memoir is that CJP, Leni and fellow BLD Treasury Ministry couples built and donated the 'Christ the Redeemer' statue at the portico of the Mirador Shrine -- and kept the donation anonymous for 30 years until Fr. Jose Quilongquilong SJ found them and asked them to go public. On June 8, 2019 -- the 30th year -- simple ceremonies rededicated the statue with a marker at its foot and a short scroll at the Retreat House hallway. For CJP, Mirador is synonymous with resurrection and salvation: since 1986, 'we have never experienced any more problems that could not be overcome with prayers of surrender to our Lord Jesus Christ, who by His own suffering, death and resurrection made it possible for us to enjoy the joy of Christian marriage.'

one_paragraph_summary: Written April 27, 2018 as the Foreword to ADL's book of speeches, this tribute by CJP identifies LOVE -- 'his enormous, googolplex love' -- as the one word that best personalizes Alberto 'Bert' David Lina. The book's opening chapter ('things my professors never taught me') acknowledges that most successful entrepreneurs never depended on college education -- Henry Sy, John Gokongwei, George Ty, Injap Sia, Steve Jobs and Bill Gates all dropped out -- and that Bert's BSBA with honors and CPA credentials are honorable but not his secret: the school of hard knocks, grit, patience, determination, and God's care are. Two threads bind his deepest thoughts: always quoting Holy Scripture to apply eternal truth to the business world, and 'love, not just like, your work.' CJP met Bert in 1969 when Bert was a young L.C. Diaz auditor examining the books of Baron Travel Corporation; from those 'peso-and-centavo days,' Bert -- born in Tondo with roots in Laguna -- rose to Filipino taipan. CJP then inventories ADL's 14 domains of love: work (18 companies including logistics, waste management, portalet systems; favorite buzz word: 'back haul'); employees (2,800 'partners and collaborators, not alalays'; free daily brown-rice meal; production bonuses regardless of rank; unused sick leave encashable); country (Customs Commissioner twice, against CJP's advice, under both GMA and Aquino III); golf, music, the poor, God (Carillon donations to five churches), daughters (April Rose, Donna May, Lucia Jane, Bertha Ann), grandchildren (only people who can countermand his orders), and above all Sylvia -- with extraordinary birthday gifts (Jaguar car, Bösendorfer piano, pink gumamela from UPLB, Sylvia P. Lina Theater at De La Salle Zobel). CJP observes that the '28' in the 28th ADL Cup refers to Bert's mythical age whenever he professes love to Sylvia, and proposes renaming the tournament ADLS -- 'Alberto Delights in Loving Sylvia.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 15, 2017 at the Vicente A. Since February 11, 2007, he has written 525 columns every Sunday without fail -- despite illness, carpal tunnel of both hands, travel abroad six times a year. On February 11, 2012 (5th anniversary of his first column), Sandy texted that WDR1 ranked 3rd on Amazon's courts bestseller list behind Jeffrey Toobin and Justice Scalia. WDR2 covers 2011 to mid-2016, supervised by J.V. Rufino, with a Foreword by Dr. Raul Pangalangan (former Inquirer publisher, now ICC judge). one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 20, 2016 at the brand-new Maybank Performing Arts Theater in BGC at the end of the 'Ageless Passion' musicale staged in his honor, this closing remarks address blends humor, gratitude, and doxology. Panganiban opens by introducing his wife Leni, his five children with their spouses, and his eight grandchildren by name. He greets Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle ('the gentle Archbishop of Manila and Pope-in-waiting,' who sang rather than recited the Prayer of St. Francis as invocation), President FVR and wife Ming (who sent his book '2030 One World, One Community, One Family' with the salutation 'Dear Tiger Chief Justice Art'), and President GMA and husband Atty. Jose Miguel (who appointed him 21st CJ without interview or conversation from the JBC's 5-name short list). He discloses that December 20 is not his actual birthday (which is December 7) but the 11th anniversary of his CJ appointment, and recalls the hotel-ballroom moment when, mid-speech, someone passed him a note that he had been appointed CJ -- he froze, descended the stage, avoided media, drove with Leni to their parish church, and on bended knees thanked the Lord. He then reformulates Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer for old age: 'Lord, grant me the senility to forget the people I never liked, the good fortune to run into the people I do, and the eyesight to tell the difference,' and quotes Frank Laubach's 'Life Begins at 80' on the joys of octogenarian forgetfulness. He inventories his life at 80 -- director/adviser in 12+ corporations and 6+ foundations with near-100% attendance, six annual trips abroad, tennis and golf four times a week, gym thrice weekly, occasional dancing -- having survived 'premature death as a six-year old during World War II' to become 'a recycled octogenarian.' He closes by reciting the personal Psalm-23-echoing prayer he composed in 1995 on entering the Supreme Court, dedicating his life to God.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 16, 2016 at the Third Philippine Conference on New Evangelization (PCNE) at Cardinal Tagle's invitation -- the theme being AWA, UNAWA, GAWA and 'Malasakit sa Bayan ni Juan de la Cruz' -- this keynote by CJP (nearly 80 years old, initially hesitant) proclaims two basic truths: God's mercy felt through Catholic faith, and God's wisdom experienced through the gift of reason. The journey of faith begins with a World War II dysentery miracle at age six in Candaba, Pampanga (given up for dead; no medical care; miraculous recovery); continues through the newsboy years in Sampaloc (promising himself he would be president of the Manila Times, fulfilled in 1991 as Inquirer President); through the UST Trinity failure ('sheepishly whispered, Jesus, Mary, Joseph'; denied scholarship; went to FEU instead -- one of the best turns of his life); through meeting Fr. Michael Nolan at FEU (Student Catholic Action), then Leni Carpio at the NUS ('She wanted to be a Benedictine nun, until she met me. She taught me how to pray'); through Marriage Encounter, Life in the Spirit, reading the Bible several times and 100+ religious books, the 1991 Second Plenary Council, and ultimately Pope John Paul II's appointment as the only Filipino in the Pontifical Council of the Laity (Vatican, 1996-2001). The journey of reason parallels it: father's deathbed vow (to fulfill his frustrated law ambition); bar exams while sick, wading through knee-deep flood, wanted to quit, Salonga insisted, placed 6th; Yale scholarship granted but travel grant denied; Salonga's consolation: 'Forget graduate studies. Come and join my law office and I will teach you what I learned from UP, Harvard and Yale.' Policy applications: vigilance on the federal system proposal; the death penalty proposal 'clearly violates the Ten Commandments, as well as the sacredness of life and the dignity of the human person.' Closes: 'God will always be with us: above us to inspire us, behind us to strengthen us, before us to lead us, and within us to transform us to be another Christ. To God be the glory! Alleluia!'

one_paragraph_summary: Written August 4, 2015 as the foreword/toast to Filemon 'Jun' T. Berba Jr.'s book, this brief tribute by CJP traces a personal debt: at Mapa High School, Jun was the consistent and uncontested math topnotcher in a class of 2,000 ('our batch mates and I vied only for second place'), and his phenomenal mathematical genius was 'enough inspiration for me to aspire to be a chemical engineer' -- an ambition redirected only by CJP's strong-willed father who insisted on law. Despite their parting at different universities, CJP 'quietly and enviously tracked Jun's pursuits' through magna cum laude in electrical engineering, an MBA at Wharton, training at SGV, and top executive roles at Ayala and Lopez enterprises. Jun's book reveals an 'engineer-manager-teacher-enabler with a social conscience and with a family of achievers in love with their patriarch's patriotic pursuits.' CJP draws the governing parallel: just as Jun transformed beyond pure engineering, CJP has 'tried to become not just a legal technician who tinkers with and repairs legal imperfections -- rather, I have tried to be a social engineer who helps build our social structures, with law as my basic tool.' He closes: 'even in my own sunset years, I still strive to be the engineer that Jun Berba inspired me to be when we were just carving our lives in high school.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 17, 2015 as the Guest of Honor speech at the Rotary Club of Makati's 50th anniversary, this address by CJP -- initially reluctant to accept as he had 'retired from active public life eight and a half years ago' -- opens with an expanded tribute to President Eddie Yap: in the foreword to his book 'Stirred, Not Shaken' (launched October 13, 2014 on his 70th birthday), CJP described him as an impresario, art connoisseur, sous-chef, civic leader and bon vivant masquerading as a financial wizard and constitutionalist -- 'a master of all of them' (6Gs: gab, giving, genius); today CJP adds 2 more: gold (Golden President for the Golden Year). The speech's centerpiece is CJP's testimony that 'it was Rotary that enabled me to enter the exalted and forbidding door of the Supreme Court': on June 17, 1992, President-elect Ramos invited him to a one-on-one and offered the Secretary of Justice post (declined); Ramos then offered the SC, revealing he had observed CJP 'closely during my Rotary presidency' and was impressed by his printed workbook (vision, mission, values, projects, work plan) and by their seatmate conversations about law and good government -- 'I know you did not campaign for me. You did not even vote for me. You voted for your mentor, Jovy Salonga. But that is alright. What matters is I know you to be competent, honest and honorable.' The moral: 'love your seatmate during Rotary meetings. He may just change your career, as Rotarian Eddie Ramos did to the career of Rotarian Art Panganiban. Who knows, Eddie Yap may turn out to be the Eddie Ramos in the life of every Makati Rotarian!' He then endorses the 50th anniversary project -- an Air Quality Monitoring and Reporting System at five Metro Manila locations (pilot: P600,000; full country: P6 million; 120 members at P50,000 each) -- and hands President Eddie a P50,000 check on the spot: 'so that my endorsement will not be only lip service.'

CJP recalls his lifelong Bedan aspiration: headed from Cataluna Street to San Beda to enroll in law, but 'intercepted when already in front of FEU by Dean Jovito R. Salonga who led me in'; his dream fulfilled only when Ave proclaimed him honorary member 'by roaring acclamation, not by quiet balloting.' He tracks Ave's career arc: youngest bar topnotcher in history at 20; LLM at Michigan at 24; Mobil general counsel at 28; ACCRA founding partner at 31 -- alongside his musical parallel (composer of ACCRA, San Beda and ALA hymns, plus 'passionate love songs to win the reluctant heart of Helen Canave'). Panganiban and Reynato S. Puno.' In thanksgiving for this inadvertent gift, CJP campaigned for Ave to become ALA President (attained February 2015); 'he now lords over six Asean Chief Justices who are his vice presidents.' But the supreme tribute: 'his greatest achievement is not in law, or in music, or in public service. Not even in ALA. In my humble opinion, his greatest achievement is convincing Helen to become his wife 50 years ago, and persuading her to repeat her sweet Yes annually during the last 50 years.' Closes with a toast and cheeky wish for another 50 years -- 'and may they celebrate tonight by adding a new member of the Cruz family who will greet the world nine months from now.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 13, 2014 at the dinner of the Asian Conference on the Family -- at the invitation of CBCP President Archbishop Socrates B. Villegas and overall coordinator Ambassador Tita de Villa -- this address by CJP speaks to the Charter of Rights of the Family tenet that the family is 'a community of love and solidarity, uniquely suited to teach and transmit cultural, ethical, social, spiritual and religious values.' He acknowledges that his personal story is already known to many in the audience but condenses his four-arc testimony: from newsboy to Inquirer president; from Catholic ignoramus to Vatican lay councillor; from failed Yale applicant to father of five children each finishing graduate degrees at Harvard, Stanford, UC, Chicago and Michigan; from aspiring chemical engineer to Chief Justice. He adds a fifth arc not often told: 'just when I thought my professional career was over... I began a new journey when I was invited to be an independent director of some of the biggest and finest listed corporations in the country. Retirement really meant getting new tires for a new journey.' The tapestry argument is then expanded: 'God has woven my many pains and gains, my frustrations and liberations, my sorrows and joys into a magnificent tapestry... but the values and blessings brought by the Lord cannot be for me only. Not even for my wife and my children only. Indeed, they must extend to my grandchildren and great grandchildren-to-be.' Applying the Charter's test: 'unless this success... is imbibed by and transmitted to the young of my family, then I may have journeyed in vain.' He invites his eldest grandchild, Jose Miguel Panganiban Sandejas -- 'now 24 years old... orphaned by his father when he was barely two years old' -- to share his own testimony of how 'our Lord turned his pains into gains, and his frustrations into liberation.' CJP reports that Miguel's sharing 'about faith, family and the grace of God moved all of us this evening.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 9, 2014 as the welcome address at the reopening of the Manila Cathedral-Basilica after two years of retrofitting and restoration, this speech by CJP -- as Foundation President, on behalf of Chairman Cardinal Tagle, Vice Chair Ambassador Tita de Villa, Treasurer Marixi Prieto, and Executive Director Monsignor Nestor Cerbo -- opens with a Tagalog greeting to President Benigno Aquino III (with sisters Ballsy, Viel and Kris), Senate President Franklin Drilon and Mila, and Mayor Joseph Estrada and Senadora Loi (CJ Sereno sent regrets, presiding over SC summer sessions in Baguio). Major donors San Miguel Group (Ramon Ang) and Metrobank Group (George Ty, Justa Lee, Antonio Oppen) are acknowledged. Representatives of the 92 parishes of the Archdiocese of Manila (10 per parish) and Caritas (representing the underprivileged, infirm and disabled) are welcomed. CJP delivers a brief theological interlude on 'church': the material structure exists to serve the community of faithful 'called by God to love Him and to love one another in worship, spirit and truth'; the cathedral is the ecclesia caput et mater omnium ecclesiarum, its cathedra (the archbishop's chair) symbolizing apostolic succession and distinguishing it from a parish church or chapel. The Cathedral was founded in 1581, damaged eight times, and rebuilt eight times -- 'the 8th and latest time' being the restoration just completed by contractor DM Consunji and project manager SP Castro. CJP notes that restoration is not yet complete: the 13-bell carillon donated by Bert and Sylvia Lina will be replaced by them with a new 23-bell set from the Netherlands 'in a few months,' and the 'antiquated air conditioning system will have to be changed as soon as we find a kind donor.' The program: audio-visual on the retrofitting; then full lights; Eucharistic Celebration presided by Cardinal Tagle with bishops and pastors; simple repast at Plaza Roma; reception at Arzobispado de Manila for donors and guests.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 28, 2014 at the investiture of Dr. Michael M. Alba as the 11th President of the Far Eastern University, this address by CJP opens by modifying the standard introduction -- 'I became the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines because I am an FEU graduate!' -- and notes that only five Philippine schools have produced Chief Justices: UP, UST, Manila Law College, Ateneo de Manila and FEU. He recalls his FEU origin: missed UP due to the 15-centavo bus fare barrier; enrolled at FEU which 'granted me a scholarship, no questions asked.' Four life-shapers met at FEU: (1) Arts and Sciences Dean Alejandro R. Roces (at 37, later the youngest Secretary of Education); (2) Law Dean Jovito R. Salonga, who 'taught me what I call the FEU model of legal education' -- a synthesis of his own UP (basic law), Harvard (master's) and Yale (doctoral) insights; (3) Fr. Michael Nolan (FEU Chaplain; taught CJP the rudiments of Catholic faith; CJP helped build the FEU Chapel in return); and (4) President Teodoro Evangelista (19 years, 1952-1971; noticed and encouraged CJP despite being one of 36,000 students). FEU gave CJP student leadership opportunities: first sophomore president of the FEU Central Student Organization; co-founder and head of NUSP (still the largest national student organization). He personally knows all six FEU presidents after Evangelista (Reyes Jr., J.C. Reyes, Sta. Maria, De Jesus, Echauz) but only met Dr. Alba last month when introduced by FEU Board Chair Aurelio Montinola III. In one hour, Alba impressed him as 'perceptive, knowledgeable, purpose-driven, humble and possessed of distinct educational ideas designed for the 21st century; his ideas blended the legacies of the past with the exigencies of the present and the hopes of the future.' With Stanford PhD, DLSU/UP economics professorship, Philippine Economic Society presidency, and World Bank/ADB/USAid consulting experience, 'Dr. Alba is the right man for the right job at the right time for the right institution.'

Ding Sanchez and Sister Lulu Carrasco; accepted because BLD shepherd Bai de los Reyes called Leni and CJP could not refuse ('Bai and her late husband Sonny were our shepherds when we entered BLD in 1986... the Lord's instruments in bringing me back to Christ... what could I have answered her? Nothing at all, except to say Amen') -- this address opens with a just-returned anecdote from Czestochowa, Poland where Fr. Simon described Cardinal Tagle as 'the Karol Wojtyla of Asia.' CJP presents the good-news-bad-news parable (a medieval farmer's horse runs away, returns with ten wild horses; son breaks leg, is spared from a war that kills all able-bodied men; farmer's response each time: 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep trying my best and God will do the rest') as the governing theological framework. He applies it to his own life: the UST Trinity failure, the Yale denial, and -- most fully told -- the seven JBC rejections (1992-1994). In January 1995, after failing seven times: 'Take oh Lord, all that I am, all that I will ever be. Take my personal ambition, my liberty, my career.' On the morning of Sunday July 30, 1995, serving as Special Minister of Holy Communion, he heard Luke 11:1-11: 'Ask and you shall receive... whoever knocks is admitted' -- 'I had cold perspiration and goose pimples.' One week later: Luke 9:28-36: 'This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him.' At the JBC meeting of September 13, 1995: 'there was a serious attempt to vote me out... no one by some mysterious reason objected'; for the first time in three years, he miraculously passed. Ramos called and asked: 'How did you do it? How did you get the JBC to nominate you?' CJP's answer: 'I did not do it. The Lord did it. Hallelujah!' After Chief Justice, he lists 12 post-retirement corporate boards (Meralco, PLDT, BPI, Metrobank, Petron, GMA Network, First Philippine Holdings, Jollibee, MPIC, Metro Pacific Tollways, Robinsons Land, Asian Terminals) and closes with the five arcs and 'To God be the glory.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 18, 2012 as an introduction of CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno as the 24th Chief Justice of the Philippines, this address by CJP opens with the most charming anecdote in the corpus: his eight-year-old granddaughter Nicole Manalac brought homemade blueberry muffins and said she would 'no longer take up law and will just be a baker because I can no longer be the first lady chief justice'; CJP replied: 'you can be the first baker in the world to become chief justice.' He greets President Fidel Ramos with the most personal Ramos tribute in the corpus: 'I owe my SC appointment to him'; during the 1992 one-on-one, Ramos acknowledged 'I know you did not even vote for me -- you voted for your mentor, Jovy Salonga -- but I want to be President not only of those who voted for me'; and crucially: 'President Ramos never spoke with me about any matter in the Supreme Court, even when I voted against some of his projects. Such is the gentleman that he is.' He praises Senator Drilon for declining the CJ aspirations out of delicadeza (after participating in the previous occupant's impeachment trial) and Senator Angara for declining Marcos's 1982 CJ offer to honor the insider tradition. He accounts for his role in Sereno's appointment: he first met her when retired Justice Florentino Feliciano brought her to his home for the NAIA Terminal III arbitration consultation; on July 30, 2010 at the GMA7 60th anniversary at the Makati Shangri-La, he introduced her to President Aquino as 'a super lawyer-economist'; Sereno reminded P-Noy of her JPEPA briefing; 'After P-Noy winked at me, I felt she instantly won the President's nod.' She was appointed a few days later as P-Noy's first SC appointee. He describes the generational change: youngest associate justice at 50 under the 1987 Constitution; 20 total years in the SC; 18 as first woman CJ (second only to Cayetano Arellano's 19 years); 12th in seniority and the most junior to become chief; chief during four presidential terms. The insider-outsider balance makes her ideal for reform. He closes: 'my hope and dream is to be alive 18 years from now when I would be 93 years old, and she, at age 70, would be retiring and proudly bequeathing to our country a truly transparent, accountable, excellent and trustworthy judiciary.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 29, 2012 at the formal launch of 'With Due Respect' (WDR1) published by the Philippine Daily Inquirer, this address by CJP thanks four speakers: Ave Cruz (ACCRA Law Chairman; close friend for half a century; declined Cory Aquino's SC offer in 1986 -- 'there would have been no Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. and Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban'); CJ Hilario Davide (predecessor; gave CJP the APJR committee chairmanship; 'most well-rounded government background' of any jurist); Aurelio Montinola III (BPI President; past Bankers Association president; CJP as BPI independent director); and Washington SyCip (91 years old; 'still robust physically and intellectually; speaks in cadenced phrases, choosing his words carefully; truly great but always humble; calls himself in his biography as Only a Bookkeeper'). He narrates the column origin: Marixi Rufino-Prieto invited him 'a few days after retirement' to write three columns a week; CJP compromised on once-weekly; 'having continuously worked since I was ten years old, I thought I was qualified to write only once a week, every Sunday.' Last year (2011), Marixi advised InqBooks would publish his selected 2007-2010 columns (chosen by John Nery) as the Prieto family's 75th birthday gift; it was made available digitally on Amazon, Apple iBook Store, iTunes and Barnes & Noble Nook. On February 11, 2012 -- exactly the 5th anniversary of his first column (February 11, 2007) -- Sandy Prieto-Romualdez texted that the book ranked #3 on Amazon's courts category, 'outranked only by the latest works of Jeffrey Toobin and US Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.' He closes with a tribute to Inquirer Publisher Isagani 'Gani' Yambot, who wrote the WDR1 Foreword but recently died unexpectedly: Gani taught CJP 'how to write simply but effectively by using plain English, with as little legalese as possible'; his WDR1 Foreword described it as 'a book written by a moral man, a Christian who not only practices the forms and rituals of his faith but who also lives it.' CJP: 'I am certain he is with us, hovering above us, joining us in spirit and in truth in our celebration.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 20, 2011 as CJP's response address at the 'Ageless Passion' musicale celebrating his 75th birthday, this speech opens with solidarity: a moment of silent prayer for the Mindanao flood victims and the eternal repose of Carolina Lapus Gozon (Henry Gozon's mother, who passed the previous night), and a P100,000 donation to Mindanao flood victims through the GMA Kapuso Foundation. Distinguished guests include VP Jejomar Binay, newly installed Archbishop Luis Antonio Tagle (who delivered the Invocation), and former Presidents Ramos and Estrada. CJP thanks the musicale team: producer Donna May Lina Flavier (Ube Media), director Bart Guingona, Ryan Cayabyab (seven original compositions), Jeff Agustin (lyrics -- former creative artist in CJP's SC Chambers, now at the University of Westminster, who traveled from the UK for the occasion), Jeffrey Solares (MSO arrangements), and Maestro Arturo Molina (MSO). He thanks his family performers: eldest grandson Miguel (narrator), granddaughters Patricia, Katrina, Victoria, Alexandra Hannett, Andrea and Nicole Manalac, Rafa Yaptangco, son Archie (a Citigroup NYC director who gave 'a passionate rendition of Rachmaninov's Concerto No. 2'), and youngest daughter Mabel (flew from NYC for the Welcome Remarks) -- and above all Leni, 'my wife of 50 years, who inspired, labored and made possible this stupendous musical miracle.' He announces that 'With Due Respect' just came off the press yesterday. Most consequentially: FLP was incorporated two months ago; its board includes CJ Davide, Washington Sycip and Edilberto de Jesus; CJP is donating five million pesos -- 'half of the entire retirement pay I received from the Supreme Court' -- to kick off fundraising. He lists 12 post-retirement corporate directorships and notes that the new journey 'breathed new meaning and purpose into my seventies.' Closes: 'To God be the glory. Merry Christmas to all of you.'

one_paragraph_summary: Published October 20, 2011, this address by CJP elaborates on his Valedictory Address of December 6, 2006 where he paid tribute to Fr. Michael Nolan ('now in the Great Beyond') as the FEU chaplain and archdiocesan director of the Student Catholic Action who 'introduced me to our Lord,' and to Fr. James Sheehy (his Columban successor who baptized all five Panganiban children). The explanation requires his full secular-upbringing narrative: born Catholic but raised without faith (parents not steeped in their own); public schools; no faith to comfort him during the child-labor years; UST Trinity failure ('Jesus, Mary, Joseph'); enrolled at FEU 'no questions asked.' At FEU, Fr. Nolan -- under whose watch the FEU Chapel was built -- 'took a personal interest in me and in what I did,' recruited him into the Student Catholic Action and taught him the rudiments of Catholicism. Fr. Sheehy added: 'a good Catholic must not only be personally pure, but must also lead others to purity; in short, be a Christ to others.' Fr. Nolan supported CJP's student leadership, helping him become the youngest and first sophomore FEU CSO President, then egging him on to organize NUSP -- and crucially, helping him convince elite Catholic schools (Ateneo, La Salle, Maryknoll, Holy Spirit, St. Scholastica's, UST, San Carlos, San Agustin) to leave their 'sheltered cocoons' and join NUSP ('FEU bolted the then existing national student organizations which were suspected to be communist fronts'). The most consequential protection: 'I was most fortunate that when I was elected FEU CSO President, Fr. Nolan was already my spiritual adviser. Otherwise, given my reformist streak, I could have joined the extremist groups' led by Jose Ma. Sison and Satur Ocampo. Through NUSP, CJP met Leni Carpio (St. Scholastica's; 'a fabled courtship'). Later: Bukas Loob sa Diyos (mid-1980s), Second Plenary Council (1991), Pontifical Council for the Laity (Vatican, 1996-2000). The arc: 'this ignorant poor boy who did not even know the three persons of the Holy Trinity became an adviser of the Holy Father. I consider this a pure gift from the Almighty.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 3, 2011 as a tribute toast for Secretary of Foreign Affairs Albert F. Del Rosario and Ambassador to Japan Manuel M. Lopez, this address by CJP opens with the philosophical frame: both men left retirement because 'they are merely changing tires prior to embarking on a new journey' -- justified by the 'amortal' concept (coined by Time Magazine) that today's 70-year-olds are the equivalents of yesteryears' 50-year-olds, life expectancy increases by 2-5 years per decade, and 'happiness lies not in merely adding more years to life, but, more important, in adding life to those years.' On Manolo Lopez: CJP first met him in early 2007 (two months after retiring as CJ) over lunch with Don Oscar M. Lopez and Don Eugenio Gabby L. Lopez III, who invited him to be an independent director of First Philippine Holdings; a year later (2008), Manolo offered him another ID in Meralco (where Manolo was and still is chairman). He describes Manolo as 'privileged by birth, a populist by choice... highly principled but not haughty, self-propelled but not self-righteous, courageous but not pugnacious, prudent but not tentative, humble but not wimpy'; his Japan earthquake-tsunami response saw him personally journeying to the disaster site 'with little regard for the possible effects of radiation on his own health.' On Albert del Rosario: known for three decades via monthly dinners with CJP and the late Doming Lim; served as Philippine Ambassador to the US (2001); resigned in 2006 'when he staunchly refused to support and, in fact, opposed the then administration's plan to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and to impose emergency rule'; met CJP at PLDT and MPIC boardrooms; 'when President Aquino offered him to head the premier Cabinet post in the Foreign Service, I immediately urged him to accept.' At DFA, he 'immediately flew to the Middle East several times to personally supervise the repatriation of our OFWs trapped in the revolutions sweeping Egypt, Libya and other countries... without TV cameras, press releases, fanfare and glitter.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 12, 2010 as the welcome address on behalf of the Manila Metropolitan Cathedral-Basilica Foundation at the 5th organ concert featuring the Cathedral's renovated giant pipe organ, this address by CJP opens with the governing theological frame: 'More than mortar and brick, the Manila Cathedral is a symbol of our faith and a monument of our religious heritage as a people. It is the bulwark of Filipino Catholicism and an enduring witness to the strength and depth of our people's fidelity to our Lord Jesus Christ.' He traces the Cathedral's history from its 1581 founding through typhoons, earthquakes, fire and WWII ('practically ravaged it to the ground'); the current Neo-Romanesque Byzantine structure was designed by Architect Fernando Ocampo and reconstructed after WWII by Archbishop Rufino J. Santos -- who became the first Filipino Cardinal -- and consecrated December 7, 1958 under the patronage of Mary, the Immaculate Conception. Now, 50+ years after reconstruction, major renovation is needed; the Foundation is chaired by Cardinal Rosales. Recent work: the giant belfry bells were brought down for earthquake safety and housed at ground level (with Dr. Emilio T. Yap's funding; to be finished November 20, 2010). And: 'the Foundation has been the fortunate recipient of the generosity of Alberto and Sylvia Lina who donated almost five million pesos to acquire new computerized, top-of-the-line carillon bells from the Netherlands. They will arrive next month, so we can use them during the Christmas season. Maraming, maraming salamat po to my inaanak, Bert and Sylvia of Fedex and Air 21 fame.' The concert program features choirs from UST, St. Paul's, St. Scholastica's, Santa Isabel and the Manila Cathedral Choir (coordinated by Eugene de los Santos and Monsignor Nestor Cerbo), composers-organists Buenaventura and Santiago, dance groups (Shirley Halili, St. Dominic, Pamana), and TV coverage by NBN Channel 4 for the Feast of the Immaculate Conception.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 21, 2010 as a birthday tribute for Manuel 'Manolo' M. Lopez at his Copa celebration -- requested by Leony de la Llana, the 'brains and baton-wielder' -- this address by CJP draws on three years of close observation as an independent director. He first met Manolo in early 2007 (two months after retiring as CJ), when Manolo and the Lopez patriarchs Oscar M. Lopez and Gabby L. one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 14, 2009 as the keynote address at the book launch of Senator Jovito R. Salonga's 'The Faith and Love of My Parents and Brothers' -- 'his invitation is really a command, a direct order from a superior' -- this address by CJP opens by noting that while Salonga has authored over a dozen books, this is his first about his immediate family; all of them remained low profile, his children barred from any appointive or elective posts while he held public office ('passionately fighting political dynasties'). CJP narrates his first encounter with Salonga: the 1956-57 FEU law student strike (1,500 students protesting the 'precipitate retirement' of Dean Lavides); new 36-year-old Dean Salonga (bespectacled Yale/Harvard graduate, bar topnotcher) walked to the microphone, spoke with a 'forceful tremolo,' and in 30 minutes sent them all back to class 'convinced of the wisdom, honesty, sincerity and good faith of their new dean.' 'I was ignited by the Yale approach.' His Yale scholarship was granted but the US Embassy denied travel funds; 'looking back, I have no regrets because Dr. Salonga invited me to join his law firm.' The book reveals that Salonga met his wife Lydia Busuego on the SS Marine Lynx en route to Harvard; they married February 14, 1948 (Valentine's Day); his Yale doctoral thesis received the highest grade possible and his private international law dissertation won the Ambrose Gherini prize -- both later converted into the most-read Filipino textbooks on corporation law and private international law. CJP quotes his Valedictory Address (December 6, 2006): Salonga is 'the one person outside of my immediate family who has had the longest and perhaps the deepest influence in my life, career and faith'; his foremost teaching: 'while it is desirable to have the necessities that money can buy, never ever forget that it is far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 21, 2008 as a testimonial toast at an ALA event for CJ Reynato S. Puno -- following his proclamation as the UP Alumni Association's Most Distinguished Alumnus during the UP centenary; CJP had proposed the ALA testimonial at the last ALA meeting and it was unanimously agreed -- this address by CJP opens by concurring with the 'Shakespeare of the Supreme Court' title but noting that Puno actually excels the English bard: 'Was it not Shakespeare who wrote, The first thing we do is to kill all lawyers?' He offers four Puno quotations as evidence: (1) 'UP taught us that on crucial issues, a UP alumnus has no right to be wrong'; (2) 'The Constitution is the refuge not only of the worthy, but also of the worthless; it is the fortress not only of the strong, but also of the weak'; (3) 'This country does not belong to the powerful. Nor does it belong to the greedy. It belongs to the Filipino whose spirit calls for honesty, for fairness, for justice, for liberty and for prosperity'; (4) in Filipino at Rizal's birthday in Calamba: 'ang kapayapaan ay hindi lamang ang kawalan ng dumadagundong na digmaan. Ito rin ay nakasalalay sa pagkakaroon ng katarungan sa lipunan' -- making Puno 'not only a Shakespeare; he is also a Balagtas.' Before 1995, CJP knew Puno only as 'a distant star'; since joining the SC, intimately. In his 1997 book 'Justice and Faith': 'Like a trained surgeon, he uses his pen with laser-like precision to separate and excise fabrication from truth and pretension from reality... Daring, gutsy and erudite, he oftentimes wages lonely battles against conventional wisdom.' In oral arguments, 'he is at once the terror of lawyers but the authority for his colleagues.' CJP's governing tribute principle: 'the greatest accolades to Chief Justice Puno come not from those who always agree with him, but from those who, from time to time, disagree with him honestly and sincerely but are convinced of the nobility of his intentions, the clarity of his thought and the inevitability of his logic.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 22, 2008 as the invocation at the 88th birthday celebration of Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, this bilingual prayer by CJP opens in Filipino: 'Manalangin po tayong lahat. O Panginoong makapangyarihan, sinasamba ka namin... Alam naming kasama Ka namin ngayon sa tahanang ito, ang tahanang pinagpala Mo at ipinagkaloob sa aming mahal na Pinuno ng Senado Jovito at Ginang Lydia Salonga.' It transitions to English for the national petitions: 'peace and prosperity in our land, sagacity and integrity for our leaders, dignity and solidarity for our people. We pray for a nation of believers, where the weak shall be strong, and the strong shall be just and the just shall be compassionate.' The centerpiece is the things-money-cannot-buy thanksgiving: CJP gives thanks for material blessings (food, clothes, homes, cars, travel) but 'even more for inculcating in us the essentials that money cannot buy like a compelling conscience that is sensitive to rectitude and propriety, love of country that transcends kinship and friendship, pursuit of excellence that is relentless and dauntless and moral courage to do what is right, regardless of personal consequences.' The Salonga birthday petition: 'Bless him O Lord with a healthy body, a robust mind, a joyful spirit and a dogged endurance to lead our country during these troubled times and to point to our confused people the way to truth, justice and peace. Anoint him with Your Spirit that he may continue to emulate Your Son, Jesus Christ, humble, upright, obedient and faithful to Your word and Your will.' The prayer closes with an unscheduled petition for victims of Typhoon Frank, 'especially the ill-fated passengers of MV Princess of the Stars that sunk off the coast of Romblon yesterday' -- the passenger ship disaster of June 21, 2008 that entered the birthday celebration's opening prayer.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 14, 2008 as a birthday toast for Charo Santos-Concio -- congratulating her as the first woman to head a major television network in the Philippines or anywhere else in the world -- this address by CJP is structured around the repeated anaphora: 'To say that Charo is [beautiful / intelligent / the boss] is to say the truth. But not the whole truth.' Beauty: 'does not come merely from the contours of her face or the sparkle of her eyes... It comes from the deepest recesses of her being. I do not merely behold her, I bathe in the glow of her sunshine; I drink of her like sweet wine and then relish the stupor of my merry drunkenness.' Intelligence: 'mere intellectuality is barren, stale, unexciting, even boring. But Charo is riveting, tantalizing, enervating, uplifting. When she moves she projects, when she writes she persuades, when she whispers she entrals, when she speaks she convinces.' Leadership: 'she does not merely command. She envisions, she inspires, she teaches, she leads... She shows how it is done. She explains why it is done. She makes her people believe in themselves. She helps them overcome their puny limitations. She enables them to excel beyond themselves.' On being the first woman to head a major network: 'she does not need human exhortations to achieve her vision and accomplish her mission. What I wish for her goes beyond what is humanly possible. What I wish for her is the Lord's benediction and sanctification. With humans, some things may not be possible. But with God, nothing is impossible.' He closes with a theological blessing: 'The Lord has chosen you because He loves you. All your dreams and all your hopes are always fulfilled because He is always with you, beside you, above you, within you, guiding you, blessing you, empowering you, sanctifying you, loving you, now and forever. Amen.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 23, 2008 as a birthday tribute for Alberto David Lina (Bert) at his 60th birthday / passage to senior citizenship celebration -- invited by his daughter Donna May Lina Flavier (CJP's inaanak) -- this address by CJP opens with their 39-year relationship: CJP first met Bert in 1969 when Bert was serving his first job (with honors BSBA from PSBA) on the LC Diaz audit team examining the books of Baron Travel, CJP's family business. CJP's governing one-word portrait: 'that one word is LOVE, his enormous, googolplex love.' Lina Theater). Conclusion: 'ADL means A Dynamo of Love. Happy Birthday Bert!'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 24, 2007 at the Canossian Academy in Lipa City for the Canossian Sisters' 200th foundation day, this is Panganiban's most compact autobiography. He opens with a medieval-farmer parable -- horse runs away (bad news), comes back with ten wild horses (good news), son breaks leg (bad news), king conscripts the village and only the lame son survives (good news) -- with the farmer's refrain 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep on trying my best and God will do the rest' becoming the speech's interpretive scaffolding. He then walks through his real story: post-WWII Sampaloc poverty as fourth child of an elementary-only mother and high-school-only Bureau of Lands clerk father; hawking newspapers, cigarettes, shoeshines; born Catholic but 'unchurched and uncatechized'; father vetoing his chemical-engineering dream and insisting on law; UP scholarship he could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare to claim; failed UST entrance interview when he answered 'Jesus, Mary, Joseph' instead of the Trinity; enrolling at FEU instead, which proved 'one of the best turns of my entire life' -- there he met Dean Jovito R. Salonga (whose teaching about aspiring for what money cannot buy he holds 'sacred to this day') and FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan (who taught him basic Catholicism). After Ramos offered him an SC seat on June 17, 1992, seven JBC rejections over three years followed; reading Luke 11 ('ask, seek, knock') and Luke 9 ('listen to Him') on successive Sundays gave him the courage to resubmit. On September 20, 1995, he passed JBC screening for the first time; in late 2005 he was named 21st CJ. To Sister Estela's question 'Why are you who you are now?' his answer: 'Please ask the Lord and Mother Mary. I am merely their servant.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 12, 2006 -- six days after his mandatory retirement -- as guest of honor and speaker at the TOFIL (The Outstanding Filipino) Awards hosted by Insular Life (CEO Vicente Ayllon), this is CJP's first major post-retirement public address. He explains his presence: he told Ayllon in September that he would no longer be CJ; Ayllon assured him that his retirement did not affect the invitation. His first post-retirement self-portrait: 'I may be looking forward to a life of retirement, but I am certainly not ready to settle into a life of complacency. While my knees may start to hurt once in a while when I play tennis or golf, I assure you that I can still do a mean boogie or tango. Retirement gives me the time and opportunity to invite my wife Leni to have a quiet dinner at our favorite restaurant, hold her hands and whisper sweet nothings as I did 50 years ago, when I was still a carefree swain trying to impress her.' He presents the four TOFIL awardees: Fr. Rocky Evangelista (Tuloy Foundation, street children rehabilitation); Antonio Meloto (Gawad Kalinga, homes for slum dwellers, 2006 Magsaysay awardee); Ramon Orlina (glass sculptor, proclaims Filipino genius internationally); and Socorro Ramos (NBS founder, 'feeding and shaping the minds of generations'). Their embodiment of three Es: (1) Excellence -- 'demands that we give our best... the continuous pursuit of excellence empowers us to constantly move forward'; (2) Ethics -- 'internalizing the old-fashioned principles of integrity, courage and prudence... at the end of life's long journey, it is the knowledge of having championed what is right'; (3) Eternity -- 'our life's final destiny... we will account for everything we have done... we must set our sights beyond the here and now to our life hereafter.' He closes with Salonga's teaching: 'God is not finished with us. For life is a long, continuing process. In a deeper sense, we are all in process, always in a state of becoming, always in a period of transition, since all of us are en route on some kind of never-ending journey.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered August 25, 1995 at a Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD) gathering -- two months before CJP's SC appointment -- this is his pre-judicial testimony on applying Christian faith to civic work, specifically his Rotary Club of Manila (RCM) presidency. Opening prayer: 'Lord Jesus, I pray that I may know you more clearly, and love you more dearly, so I can imitate you more nearly and serve you more eagerly.' He traces his pre-conversion arc: St. Augustine ('our hearts are restless till they rest in God'); his own path through academic honors and student leadership that 'did not satisfy my thirst for life and love, for peace and happiness'; then the pursuit of worldly wealth -- 'in the early eighties, I quickly earned over four million U.S. dollars from zero in just two years, only for this incredible wealth to vanish into thin air in the stock market crash of 1982 in Hongkong. The lavish life-style I enjoyed did not bring me peace -- it merely increased my appetite for more and more.' The 1986 turning point: Life in the Spirit Seminar; baptism in the Holy Spirit; proclamation of Jesus as Lord; BLD membership; 'I developed a hunger for Scriptures... gifts of discernment, sharing, reflection, prayer and healing.' His RCM presidency (organized June 1, 1919; oldest Rotary in Asia; 455 members; largest in Asia and the world except the US): he subjected the election to BLD discernment and prayer; won with a record margin; the Isaiah 42 confirmation; formulated the LOVE GOD SERVE MAN credo (from Mark 12:29-32); expanded it into a 76-page Program of Action with 178 projects, P90M budget (18x the previous P5M maximum). Inaugural address (July 12, 1990): 'I vow to channel our major treasures, time and talent in helping our less fortunate brothers.' At the first regular meeting, members contributed P5.5 million in 30 minutes for earthquake victims, followed by P660,000 the next day: 'I view this tremendous outpouring of support not merely as an answer to my call to LOVE GOD SERVE MAN but as a sign of His Providence when we discern and obey His will and step out in faith to proclaim it.'

His constituents betrayed Him, chanting, Crucify Him. And yet He is the only King who resurrected from the dead and by such resurrection conquered sin not just in His own time but in all eternity.' The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve -- to give His life in ransom for the many'; washing the apostles' feet; (4) Prayer and faith -- 'In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed so intensely that his sweat became like drops of blood'; teaching the Lord's Prayer; (5) Justice and love (Romans 14:17) -- the judge-daughter parable in its earliest form: a judge fines his speeding daughter P500, then removes his robe and pays the fine himself ('He paid the penalty out of love because the law-breaker was his daughter. Such is King Jesus. All hail King Jesus!'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered as a laudation at the RVR Awards Ceremony on August 20, 2024, this speech presents former Ambassador Howard Q. Dee as the personification of the late Ambassador Ramon V. Del Rosario Sr.'s twin beacons -- matchless excellence in business and extraordinary devotion to the less privileged. As President and CEO of Unilab (the Philippines' largest drug manufacturer, competing with Roche, Pfizer, J&J, Novartis, and Merck), Dee considered himself 'God's servant first and foremost' and shared CJP's credo that things money cannot buy (integrity, honor, candor, truth, trustworthiness, love for God) matter far more than things money can buy. He pioneered Philippine corporate social responsibility by co-founding PBSP with former Ambassador Bienvenido Tan Jr. -- inviting ~50 top tycoons (Sorianos of San Miguel, Eugenio Lopez Sr. of Meralco, Sixto Roxas of Bancom, Washington SyCip of SGV) to commit 1% of net income before taxes to poverty reduction; PBSP now has 230+ members led by Manuel Pangilinan. After retiring from Unilab in 1972, Dee founded the Assisi Development Foundation (named after St. Francis of Assisi, for 'quiet but stubborn devotion to empower, serve and love the poor'), chaired the government's CPP-NPA-NDF peace panel (1993-1999), served as Ambassador to the Holy See and Malta under President Cory Aquino (1986-1990), and in July 1994 co-founded ASA Philippines Foundation with Kamrul Tarafder and late banker Eduardo Go -- which by its 2022 Chairman's Message had earned P5.9 billion, served 2 million+ clients nationwide, operated 1,683 branches, employed 11,401 souls, and maintained a 93.97% repayment rate. CJP notes that FLP's Prosperity Fund co-chairs -- former BSP Governor Tetangco and retired SAJ Perlas-Bernabe -- are attending to learn ASA's microfinance model, and concludes: 'the Filipino is trustworthy, credit worthy and Christ worthy.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 28, 2023 at the FLP Awards Ceremony welcoming 21 new law scholars, 10 dissertation winners, and 5 ESMEL fellows, this speech by CJP opens by thanking CJ Gesmundo (keynote and Legal Scholarship Board of Judges chair), Kyle Tan (Tan Yan Kee Foundation, grandson of Dr. Lucio C. Tan), Fernando Zobel de Ayala (Ayala Corporation), Alfred and Cherry Ty (Metrobank Foundation), Msgr. Gerry Santos ('Nak' to CJP's 'Tay' and the late Leni's 'Nay' -- three months after Leni's April 9, 2023 death), Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, Gov. Tetangco (SM Investments Chair, first P1-trillion-cap company), Atty. Felipe Gozon (GMA -- whom CJP once invited to join the Court), World Bank executives Dandan Chen and Dave Llorito, Injap Sia (absent but donated an unsolicited P888,000 -- 'Palakpakan po natin si Injap'), and Marixi Rufino Prieto (donated a colored Inquirer ad). He presents wisdom to the scholars through his life narrative: poverty blocked his UP scholarship (15-centavo bus fare), but FEU opened the window to Salonga; a Yale scholarship was blocked by a US Embassy visa denial (due to student activism), but hard-knock education followed; each closed door opened a wider window. He also recounts producing 1,200+ decisions and one book per year at the Court, earning the unanimous 'Renaissance Jurist' resolution, before being inspired at age 75 by Cayabyab's 'Ageless Passion' to transform judicial philosophy from 'imbedded legal lore' to 'practical reality' by organizing FLP (seeded with P2 million, now over P50 million in head office and P50 million in educational projects). He unveils FLP's two ultimate projects: the immersive, AI-powered Museum for Liberty and Prosperity (visitors inside a virtual SC Session Hall; AI robots mimicking justices; Task Force headed by retired SAJ Perlas-Bernabe) and the multi-billion-peso Prosperity Fund for MSMEs (Task Force headed by Gov. Tetangco). The family's P100M+ Paseo de Magallanes lot is donated as seed money; 23 million pesos already pledged by friends. He closes: 'Liberty and prosperity must always be together -- freedom must be of the mind and of the stomach... food must be of the intellect and of the gut' and invokes Matthew 25:40 ('Whatever you do for the least of my brethren, you do unto me') as the divine mandate for the Prosperity Fund.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered August 11, 2022 as online closing remarks at FLP's Awards Ceremony -- shifted from face-to-face at AIM to virtual format because of the Omicron surge -- this speech frames the foundation's decade-transition thesis: the first decade (2011-2021) was concentrated on LIBERTY programs (Professorial Chairs with Metrobank, Scholarship with Tan Yan Kee Foundation, Dissertation Writing with Ayala); the second decade (2021-2031) will broaden into PROSPERITY programs starting with the ESMEL Fellowships at ₱450,000 each (in partnership with MPIC and MVP, MOA drafted by CFO Chaye Cabal-Revilla and bar-topper Chief Legal Counsel Jun Pilares III). CJP discloses his MPIC independent directorship as a corporate-governance modeling. He thanks CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo as Scholarship Board of Judges chair and adopts the CJ's keynote formulation -- 'safeguarding rights go hand in hand with nurturing prosperity' -- as the canonical SC-articulation of FLP's symbiotic philosophy. He thanks J. Ramon Paul L. Hernando (Dissertation Board) and Gov. Amando 'Say' Tetangco Jr. (ESMEL Board). He then announces the AIM Master in International Business Law (MIBL) curriculum, designed over 8 months with President/Dean Jikyeong Kang and faculty Olivier Roche and Felipe Calderon -- inspired by his grandson Miguel Panganiban Sandejas's unusual Babson MBA + Northwestern MSL trajectory (graduate law without undergraduate law) -- and invites Ateneo, La Salle, UP, and UST to follow AIM's lead. He acknowledges Tan Yan Kee Foundation (six years of scholarship funding, including 21-slot expansion to resolve a tie), Ayala Corporation (5 years of Dissertation Writing), Tony Tan Caktiong + Injap Sia (Hotel 101 condo donation for poor-student assistance), and Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez (Acting FLP President). He closes by announcing FLP's two ultimate projects -- the Center for Liberty and Prosperity with interactive immersive Museum (liberty side, with SC partnership) and the ₱1B+ 'Entrepreneurship Fund' for MSMEs (prosperity side, with pro bono viability study by Cezar Consing) -- and asks the audience to pray for their attainment.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 25, 2022 at the RVR Awards Ceremony, this laudation by CJP presents Dr. Tony Tan Caktiong as the 2022 RVR Award for Nation Building recipient and as 'a truly world-class Filipino entrepreneur.' CJP traces JFC's trajectory from a single mom-and-pop Chickenjoy store co-founded by Tony and Grace Tan Caktiong in 1978 to 6,000+ stores across 18 international brands (Mang Inasal, Chow King, Tim Ho Wan, Yonghe King, Smashburger, Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf) in 34 countries -- reaching top-10 QSR status globally pre-pandemic and aiming for top-5 in eight years by doubling store count and revenue. He narrates the stock-market story: listed on the PSE at P9 per share in 1993, peaking at P325 pre-pandemic (a 36x multiplier in <30 years), dropping to P100 at pandemic height, and recovering to ~P210 at the time of the speech -- prompting the parenthetical: 'It's time to buy JFC shares!' -- accompanied by his disclosure as a non-executive JFC director. He observes, humorously, that if the awardee visited one store daily and ate a meal in each, he could not finish visiting all during his lifetime because they multiply faster than visits. He praises Tan Caktiong as remaining 'humble, friendly, generous and patriotic' despite this achievement, notes the Jollibee Group Foundation's direct-sourcing model that guarantees fair mark-ups for Filipino farmers and poultry raisers, and concludes that the late Ambassador Ramon V. Del Rosario Sr. 'would surely be proud that his dream for global Filipino ingenuity and pioneering spirit is fulfilled to the hilt by our Awardee.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 13, 2021 -- the exact 10th anniversary of FLP's founding on October 13, 2011 (CJP's 75th birthday) -- this address opens with the heaven-versus-hell joke: a corrupt politician who chooses hell after being shown a campaign-promise paradise, only to find garbage and gnashing teeth on arrival. The Devil: 'Yesterday we were campaigning and promising. Today you voted for us and chose our reality.' The joke frames CJP's central thesis: slogans, promises, theories and tweets fail as poverty-alleviation tools because they are not backed by sustainable philosophies, implementable programs and realistic timelines. He traces his own near-Marxist moment as a dirt-poor political science student (acquainted with Sison and Ocampo) and his rejection of communist slogans despite their emotional appeal, citing Deng Xiaoping's One-Country-Two-Systems shift as proof that China's success came from entrepreneurship not ideology, and the South/North Korea contrast as the companion proof. He analyses the Bill of Rights' predominantly negative language ('no person shall be deprived...') as necessary but insufficient -- the positive constitutional economic goals and Jesus's two commands of love must also be implemented. He confesses a 'throbbing yearning' even after producing the most decisions in the Court's century-long history -- most were negative (stop the illegal behavior) rather than implementing positive provisions. He reports FLP's first decade: a 700-sqm Makati office, Professorial Chairs, 20 annual law scholarships (drawing scholars from Ateneo de Davao, Ateneo de Cagayan, MSU, Fr. Saturnino Urios, U Cordilleras, St. Louis, and others), dissertation writing contests, and educational assistance for the poor. He announces the second decade's centerpiece: ESMEL fellowships in MBA programs (economics, sustainability, business law, entrepreneurship) and the Entrepreneurship Fund of at least P1 billion to invest in and help manage MSMEs with social impact but no bank access -- with former BPI president Cezar Consing studying its viability pro bono. He closes hoping to be present at FLP's 20th anniversary in 2031, 'even in my wheelchair,' to celebrate 'triumph and fulfillment in the Lord's vineyard.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered August 13, 2021 at FLP's online Awards Ceremony, this closing address by CJP thanks CJ Gesmundo (Scholarship Board of Judges chair), SAJ Perlas-Bernabe (Dissertation Board of Judges chair, third time; hoped to continue after her May 2022 retirement), Secretary of Justice Guevarra (whose Sunday WhatsApp insights on CJP's Inquirer columns are eagerly anticipated), and partners Tan Yan Kee Foundation (Dr. Lucio Tan as Chairman, Harry Tan as Vice Chairman) and Ayala Corporation (Jaime Augusto Zobel). He closes with an internal-unity caveat (no partisan activities within the Society; 'minds are like parachutes -- they work only when they are open') and a haunting farewell promise: 'Though I may be already in the Great Beyond, my spirit will be hovering above you, beside you and behind you.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered February 6, 2021 as edited extemporaneous closing remarks at the online Awards Ceremony for the Fourth Year FLP Law Scholars (AY 2020-2021), this speech is structurally the most personally disclosing of CJP's FLP addresses. He thanks the FLP Board of Trustees present (Edilberto de Jesus, Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez, his wife Prof. Leni Panganiban, daughter Marilen Yaptangco, Treasurer Becky Felix, Executive Director Susan Gavino as 'mother hen'), the Tan Yan Kee Foundation (represented by Valerie Ann L. Tan, niece of Dr. Lucio Tan) for six years of unbroken Scholarship funding through COVID, and congratulates the nine fourth-year graduating scholars whose checks will be deposited the following Monday. He explains the 20-scholars-per-year program structure (10 third-year + 10 fourth-year), the Preliminary Selection Committee under Atty. Joel Gregorio, and the final-interview Board of Judges chaired by the incumbent Chief Justice or a Senior Associate Justice -- 'in the inner sanctum of the Court.' The speech's emotional center is a vulnerable personal disclosure: none of his five children and none of his ten grandchildren entered law, leaving him frustrated that his legacy 'would come to an end' -- he self-deprecatingly mentions briefly considering 'adopting young people who might become lawyers or even... donating to - what do you call that? - sperm banks' before settling on FLP as the better legacy vehicle. Forty scholars across four batches now constitute that legacy. He validates the program by reciting bar topnotchers -- Batch 1's Sean Borja (No. 1) and Katrina Gaw (No. 5), Batch 2's Kenneth Manuel (No. 6) and Dexter Rojas (No. 9) -- and previews the FLP 10th Anniversary projects (Coffee Table Book edited by Joel Gregorio with FLPSS support, funded by a ₱3M Metrobank Foundation grant, plus a separate Professorial Lectures volume) launching before October 10, 2021. He describes himself, at 84, as 'still trying to operate my laptop, my iPad, my desktop, of course, my smart cell phone.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 11, 2020 via Zoom at the first formal meeting of the FLP Scholars Society (FLPSS), this opening address by CJP -- who immediately frames the COVID-forced online format as 'a blessing' that inaugurates 'the normal things in the DiGi Age' -- offers practical founding guidance. He emphasizes FLPSS membership exclusivity (only those who passed FLP's stringent screening by SC justices and committed to the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy from the best law schools in the country), reiterates the prophetic commissioning ('in the next 10 to 20 years, you would be the leaders of our country -- chief justices, justices, legislators, cabinet members, even Presidents'), and provides specific guidance: craft Vision and Mission Statements first; the Mission should include (1) strengthening unity via a Wikipedia-style directory and minimum fees (free for undergraduates, P2,000/year for graduates), (2) giving back by recruiting future applicants and donating for more scholarships, and (3) helping FLP create new programs. He specifies the Fundamental Principles and Core Values: democracy, freedom, integrity, ethics, free enterprise, hard work, patriotism, excellence, innovation, creativity, and DiGi Age virtues. He insists on focus discipline -- the Society must NOT divert to side causes like climate change, poverty alleviation or disaster assistance, however laudable ('there would be enough people... that would take them up') -- and on internal political neutrality ('minds are like parachutes -- they work only when they are open'). He defines his own role self-deprecatingly as 'ancient lolo, alalay or assistant' (or Adviser, 'if you want to be high falutin'), invites the President to attend the July 16 FLP Board Meeting as observer, and previews two new FLP programs: ESME graduate fellowships and the Entrepreneurship Fund of about P1 billion for MSMEs. He closes with the succession vision: future FLPSS members will be elected to the FLP Board, 'because we, of the older generation, will pass away someday and will be glad to turn over gradually to you the leadership.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 28, 2019 at the UP College of Law, these closing remarks by CJP present Prof. Beth Pangalangan her P100,000 honorarium check (less 5% withholding under the TRAIN Law) and formally enroll her as a holder of one of the 15 CJ Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity -- calling her lecture 'one of the best I have ever heard in a long time... scholarly prepared and eloquently delivered' and particularly moved by her citations of his decisions, books, columns and speeches. He then personally hands Dean Fides 'Deng' Cordero Tan an on-the-spot letter of invitation to join as a chair holder -- a unanimous FLP Board resolution triggered by her reputation for excellence. He narrates his lifelong unrequited love affair with UP: in the early 1950s, he won a UP scholarship but his father (a government employee) could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare from Sampaloc to Diliman; he enrolled at nearby FEU instead; co-founded NUSP with UP Student Council President Fernando Lagua and Philippine Collegian Editor Homobono Adaza (Lagua suspended one year, Adaza expelled from UP; CJP: 'Buti na lang hindi ako nakapasok sa UP, baka expelled din ako'). His unrequited love was requited in three ways: son Archie was the 4th student to graduate summa cum laude from the UP Conservatory of Music and is now an Executive Director at JP Morgan in New York; then-UP President Angara gave him a small Oblation replica in the early 1980s as thanks for securing Japanese fire truck donations; and he was enrolled as an honorary member of Phi Kappa Phi. He describes FLP's three programs -- 15 Professorial Chairs (3 held by UP academics: Prof. Pangalangan, Dean Tan, and President Concepcion), 20 law scholarships at P200,000 each (including Frederick Ervin Dy from UP), and the Dissertation Writing Contest (with 'the illustrious son of the illustrious couple from UP and Harvard,' Raphael Pangalangan, winning the previous year's first prize of P300,000) -- and closes: 'my fervent hope for FLP's closer link and cooperation with the academics and students of the UP College of Law, the best law school in the world... according to the UP Law Alumni Association.'
