one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 1, 2016 as the closing address at the inaugural FLP Scholarship Program launch ceremony, this speech by CJP opens with profound thanks to CJ Maria Lourdes Sereno for chairing the first Board of Judges, opening the SC's three Division Conference Rooms ('normally reserved exclusively for sessions of the three Divisions... when justices convene in these hallowed halls, they meet strictly by themselves, without clerks, stenographers or secretaries'), and delivering a stimulating and challenging speech specifically addressing law school deans and the inaugural LibPros scholars -- 'amazed how she can remember so accurately the give and take between the candidates and the applicants.' He thanks the other judges: FLP President Evelyn Dumdum, Dr. Edilberto de Jesus, TYK Foundation's Maria Cecilia Pesayco, and PALS President Dean Maria Soledad Mawis of Lyceum PH. He notes the positive surprise: 'We were looking for only 10 scholars but the board of judges was so impressed by the applicants, they recommended 11. The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity happily agreed.' He sets explicit expectations for the inaugural batch: graduate with honors, be among the top 10 in the 2018 bar exam, and become 'competent and ethical lawyers who will safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity under the rule of law.' He describes FLP (founded December 2011, CJP's 75th birthday) and its programs: 20 law scholarships (11 in the first batch), dissertation contest (P300K champion, P200K 2nd, three P100K honorable mentions, P20K for 20 entries), 10 professorial chairs across eight law schools plus the Philippine Judicial Academy. He notes FLP's office: 700+ square meters in Salcedo Village, Makati, donated by First Philippine Holdings, Lopez Holdings, PLDT, Meralco, MPIC, and San Miguel Corp. president Ramon Ang. He closes with an invitation to merienda with the 11 inaugural scholars.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 19, 2012 as the closing remarks at the inaugural lecture of the FLP Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chair Series -- the first lecture delivered by Dean Sedfrey M. Candelaria at Ateneo de Manila Professional Schools -- this brief address by CJP opens with the sharpest honorarium presentation in the corpus: 'The Bible says man does not live by bread alone. And I add, neither can he live without it. So here is the check for one hundred thousand pesos for your professorial chair.' He notes that Dean Candelaria 'set a very high standard' and 'immediately lifted the issue of liberty and prosperity to the international plane.' He reflects on his lifelong Ateneo aspiration ('too poor; had to peddle newspapers and shine shoes; both parents died in college'), noting he finally got to speak at the 2006 Ateneo graduation where he predicted a bar topnotcher -- Joan de Venecia became number 1 and three Ateneo graduates made the top ten. CJ Hilario Davide Jr. is present; CJP credits him with the APJR ('so successful the World Bank placed it in its website as a model for all developing countries') and notes with regret that 'our successors in the Court did not find it good enough to be continued'; he expresses hope that incumbent CJ Sereno ('holds an economics degree from Ateneo and a law degree from UP') will continue and update it. He briefly restates his judicial philosophy (strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters) and describes the Global Forum (October 2006) where CJ Beverley McLachlin suggested adding 'Under the Rule of Law' -- then 'fell in love with the Philippines, especially with Ateneo de Manila, that she stayed four more days; Ateneo gave her a Doctoral Degree in Law, Honoris Causa. So you have a co-alumnus, the Chief Justice of Canada by the name of Beverley McLachlin.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 30, 2006 at the unveiling and signing of the foundation stone marker for the PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay -- six days before CJP's mandatory retirement -- this address recounts 'the long and tortuous journey... indeed a chronicle of faith.' The journey: July 19, 1995 -- at the instance of Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio T. Carpio, President Ramos turned over the 3.3-hectare facility to the SC; November 23, 1998 -- first cornerstone under CJ Narvasa; throughout CJ Davide's term -- pursued Japanese government funding; January 26, 2006 -- Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki handed over the strings-free P300 million grant to the Philippine government and then to the SC. PhilJA is 'the first and only training school for the Philippine judiciary'; the completed Development Center will make it a national and 'ASEAN regional hub for continuing legal and judicial education, pre-judicature training, judicial career enhancement, and various programs in specialized areas of the law.' CJP has signed judicial education cooperation agreements with Spain and Egypt; agreements with France, UK, Russia and Pakistan are being finalized. Longer-term vision: a special school for young lawyers aspiring to become career judges -- 'similar in concept and orientation to our very own Foreign Service Institute'; competitive examinations to ensure 'only the best and the brightest are trained... professional judges who will not just be steeped in the law, but also be deep in ethical and moral values.' The ACID connection: 'the intensified campaign to eradicate the corrosive effects of ACID can be waged much faster and more successfully if we start at the very foundations of judicial training and education.' Closing: 'May I invite all of you to join hands with me in building the PhilJA Development Center, our chronicle of faith and our testament of hope for a reformed judiciary.'

The history: on December 4, 2004, CJ Davide issued Administrative Circular No. 61-2004, appropriating P40M (from the Judiciary Development Fund's 20% equipment allocation) for the CA Cebu building; this was later increased to P70M in December 2005; the provincial government of Cebu donated the more than 2,000 sqm site. Three-way credit: the dream was 'initiated by Chief Justice Davide, the commitment of the present leadership of the Supreme Court, and the generous support of the provincial government of Cebu.' The governing historical metaphor: 'On April 14, 1521, the advent of Christianity in these islands was ushered in by Cebu, when King Humabon and his wife, Queen Juana, received the sacrament of baptism. In much the same way, we are once again making Cebu a gateway, this time to the judiciary. In 1521, Cebu helped spread the faith; in 2006, it facilitated access to justice.' The ACID connection: the building addresses the 'A' (Access) -- 'litigants will no longer have to bear the additional expense of flying to Manila to argue or follow up their appealed cases.' Values reminder for the 26,000 court employees: DHL (dedication, honesty, loyalty); for the nine CA Cebu justices: four Ins (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence). Closes in Cebuano: 'Daghang salamat!'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 14, 2006 at Bulacan State University -- Dr. Rosario P. Pimentel as president; Justice Jose C. dela Rama as College of Law dean -- on receiving an honorary Doctor of Laws degree, this address by CJP is delivered almost entirely in Filipino and constitutes the only full Filipino-language statement of his governance framework. He presents the four Ins in Tagalog: 'kasarinlan, katapatan, kasipagan, katalinuhan' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence). He narrates the APJR continuation and the four ACID problems (Filipino paraphrase). He states EC (competent and ethical lawyers) and DHL (dedication, honesty, loyalty for the 26,000 court employees). Crucially, he asserts the governing hierarchy: 'dagli at madalas kong sabihin na ang mga adhikaing ito ay hindi mga pangwakas na layunin, kundi mga paraan lamang upang maabot ang dalawang mas mataas na tunguhin: (1) ang pagsasanggalang ng kalayaan at (2) ang pagpapayabong sa kasaganaan ng ating mga mamamayan.' He states the liberty standard (timbangan ng katarungan laban sa pamahalaan, pabor sa mga dukha) and the prosperity standard (pitagan at paggalang sa Panguluhan at Kongreso). He closes: 'Alam kong di ko makikita nang buo ang katuparan ng mga saloobin kong ito, subali't ako'y lubos na nananalig na ang binhi ay naitanim ko na. Sa pamamagitan ng ating pagdadaupang palad at pagtitipon ngayon, sana'y tulungan ninyo akong palaganapin sa buong bayan at sa buong mundo, ang bagong ebanghelyo ng KALAYAAN at KASAGANAAN.'

On access to justice: the Justice on Wheels program (deployed December 21, 2004; a mobile court bus with judge, prosecutor and stenographer, initially for Family Court cases in the NCR; two more buses ordered for Visayas and Mindanao). On corruption and incompetence: strict entrance and promotion requirements, continuing ethical education, and doubled compensation per RA 9227. The father exclaimed: This is the one who will lead.' Application: 'sometimes it takes so little to accomplish so much of a gargantuan task. I urge all of you to take courage in lighting your own little candles of reform in your respective courts and together, we shall light up the firmament of justice in our country.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 5, 2006 at Angeles University Foundation on receiving an honorary Doctor of Laws degree -- with retired Justice Jose C. Vitug (fellow Kapampangan) as founding dean of the new AUF College of Law -- this address by CJP opens by noting Pampanga's development: 'Pampanga is in the cusp of development. Yet, not too long ago, many feared its economic regression after the Americans pulled out from Clark Air Base, and after the destructive eruption of Mt. Pinatubo in 1991. Since then, the Clark Special Economic Zone has replaced the American base' -- 'a testimonial to the Pampanguenos' resilience and fortitude.' He introduces the new AUF College of Law with Vitug as dean and expresses confidence its graduates will reach the bar's top ten. He presents Jose Abad Santos as the supreme embodiment of the four Ins: 'born in San Fernando, Pampanga, February 19, 1886; became SC justice in 1932; secretary of justice in 1938; captured by Japanese in Barili, Cebu, April 11, 1942; adamantly refused to cooperate with the military conquerors; before execution, his parting words to his son: Don't cry. What is the matter with you? Show these people that you are brave. It is a rare opportunity to die for one's country, and not everybody is given that chance. Thus, he died a martyr and hero.' CJP's interpretation: 'Chief Justice Abad Santos lived and died by an ideal magistrate's standards, which I have referred to in many past speeches as the four Ins: independence, integrity, industry and intelligence. Integrity is not limited to mere honesty and truthfulness; it entails acting in accordance with what is true and honest regardless of personal consequences. Integrity requires the moral courage to stand for one's convictions against all odds.' Two months from retirement: 'I look forward to retirement with tranquility and contentment over the thought that I shall leave behind an energized breed of Pampangueño magistrates who personify the four Ins; who continue to battle the ACID problems of our justice system; and who champion the loftier cause of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity! Dacal pung salamat.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 27, 2026 at the Main Lounge of the Manila Polo Club, 40 days after Linda Manuel Mañalac's passing on March 21, 2026, this eulogy by CJP -- himself a three-year widower following Leni Panganiban's sudden death on April 9, 2023 -- opens by thanking Fr. Francis Alvarez SJ for the yoke parable (Christ as the strong ox bearing more of the burden) and frames the address through the 'fragility of life' theme: Linda was in and out of Makati Med ICU for three months, pronounced healed and ready for discharge, then died unexpectedly. CJP builds a cumulative named-witness canon -- Linda's son Carlos 'Pop' Mañalac on her 'complete, absolute, unconditional generosity'; common granddaughter Andrea on her presence at every important moment; nephew Rico Manuel (Ayala Land) on Ninang Linda as 'the glue that held our family together'; Sonya Garcia on the day Linda paid the full price for the undeveloped Alfonso, Cavite estate (that became Sonya's Garden) without inspecting it; Sister Cho Borromeo on 30 years of Linda hosting the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary (25 in Pasay + 5 in Forbes Park); Fr. Robert Manansala on Linda's love for God, family, the Southeastern College community, and the poor; and even Tagaytay-road street vendors of boiled corn and camote. He distills this as 'Generosity Personified' and, in his own coinage, 'Love and Magnanimity Magnified.' His personal reminiscences include the pearl-necklace gift Linda gave at her own birthday party to a first-time-met retired SC justice ('There, bagay na bagay sa iyo'), Punta Fuego fishermen waiting because she paid above asking price, and the 'Happy Foursome' / 'Sousai 100 Travel and Gourmet Barkada' travels of Tong & Linda Manalac with Tony & Leni Panganiban through Morocco, the Danube, San Francisco, Rome, Madrid, Paris, Saigon, and Hong Kong. He frames Linda's spirituality as Ignatian deed-over-word -- 'giving without counting the cost' -- and closes with an explicit public promise to fellow-widower Tong ('walking and breathing the fresh morning air at the Manila Polo Oval... Hacienda Linda... beaches of Batangas... gold tees of Manila Golf... shell courts of Manila Polo'), generalized as a pastoral exhortation to all widows and widowers to 'look back on the past with gratitude and quiet surrender' and to live fully until 'a joyful reunion with them, together with all His angels, in His Heavenly Kingdom.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 16, 2024 at the National Museum of Fine Arts during the 1971-72 Constitutional Convention Surviving Delegates' Conference and Exhibits on 'Philippine Constitutions and the Social Order,' this speech opens with an admission against interest ('I do not feel qualified... I AM NOT A ROBOT') and a joke about three new commandments added by scheming lawyers and unfaithful husbands ('Thou shall not get caught'; 'deny, deny, deny, even when caught in flagrante'; invoke the right to remain silent). Borrowing the judicial opinion structure (FACTS -- ISSUE -- RULING), CJP situates the 1987 Constitution -- ratified February 2, 1987 and in force February 11, 1987 -- within the global 'AI Winter' of 1973-1993, demonstrating with the ILOVEYOU virus case (May 2000, $5B+ damages, two Filipino programmers acquitted because PH had no anti-malware law) that constitutional anticipation of technology was structurally impossible. He then enumerates seven contemporary pressure points: (1) in vitro fertilization and surrogacy (citing Pope Francis's January 8, 2024 ambassadors speech calling surrogacy 'despicable'); (2) nanotechnology's dual nature; (3) autonomous weapons that select targets without human intervention; (4) cyber risks and AI errors in the hands of terrorists, dictators, and warlords; (5) social-media-driven youth suicide (more US young people die by suicide than by soldiers/terrorists/criminals combined); (6) the illusory truth effect in political ads ('Saligang Batas Gawing Saligang Patas' with 1M+ X views); and (7) the 100% Filipino-mass-media ownership constraint in an era of CNN/BBC and foreign social platforms. His ruling: humane justice can be dispensed ONLY by judges, not by automated formula -- the Penal Code's range of penalties and the Civil Code's 'right and justice' liberality clause confer discretion irreducible by tech bots. He cites the UK House of Lords March 30, 2022 'Technology Rules?' report ('a new Wild West'), the November 2023 Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit (29 governments including the Philippines), and US CJ Roberts's 2023 Year-End Report confirming judges are not becoming obsolete. He endorses CJ Gesmundo's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027 -- 'turn tech for good and move from problem to solution' -- as the right institutional posture, and closes by invoking the 1987 Constitution's preamble guarantee of human dignity 'especially the poor, the oppressed, the dispossessed, the weak, the disabled and the marginalized' as the irreducible reference point for all technology policy.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 9, 2023 at the Makati Shangri-La as extemporaneous closing remarks of the MVP Group's Annual Corporate Governance Enhancement Session, this short address showcases CJP's witty register at a corporate-governance audience. Opening with a self-deprecating mock-rank-comparison -- he is not the great MVP (Manuel V. Pangilinan) but a 'lowly AVP' (Artemio V. Panganiban), a 'fake' -- he punishes the audience with 'I'll prolong my talk so you won't eat,' then performs an object-anecdote with a borrowed Grand Hyatt ballpen used to take notes at the Makati Shangri-La event, borrowed from the Grand Hyatt's owner Alfred Ty seated beside him. He thanks guest lecturer Dr. Max Tegmark and panel reactor Paco Sandejas (disclosing the family tie: Paco is the brother of CJP's deceased son-in-law Thomas Sandejas; Paco and CJP's son both UP summas and Stanford PhDs). He then delivers three takeaways: (1) invest in human intelligence as contradistinguished from AI -- 'artificial intelligence is fake, human intelligence is real. So, we will invest in all of you, in all your brains. We will just make AI our slave'; (2) customer-centricity as North Star -- 'we will use artificial intelligence, native intelligence, Filipino intelligence, PLDT intelligence to serve our customers'; and (3) leverage the MVP Group's collective strength across PLDT, Meralco, Maynilad, MPH, and tollways. He closes by posing the governance questions the executives must answer -- customer data protection, transactional integrity, cybersecurity, and respectful competition -- and asks: 'Are we up to the challenge?'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 12, 2020 -- Independence Day -- as the closing address at FLP's first pandemic-era online awards ceremony, this speech by CJP opens with thanks to CJ Diosdado Peralta and SAJ Estela Perlas-Bernabe (Board of Judges chairs) and the Tan Yan Kee Foundation and Ayala Group, and acknowledges that bar exams have been postponed by COVID. The governing philosophy is the 'little things' thesis, illustrated by two stories. The first is Lucila Takjerad's Harvard commencement: a 1994 Algerian civil war refugee's illiterate mother couldn't write her name on the French emigration list; a stranger scribbled it; the family emigrated to France; Lucila graduated Harvard and proposed: 'Fellow graduates, of course, do the most you can do... But also do the least you can do. Because, the least you can do might turn out to be the most significant.' The second is CJP's own story: both parents dead, no money for bar review, an anonymous older friend paid for it on condition he land in the Top Ten; CJP was hospitalized during the first bar Sunday but Salonga urged him not to quit; he landed sixth place. The friend 'never knew how his simple gesture... brought me over to the noble legal profession and, eventually, to the highest judicial position in our country.' CJP positions FLP's own programs -- grants, SC interviews, board questioning, midnight dissertation-writing, secretariat kindness -- as the institutionalized version of that stranger's gesture. He then addresses the AI challenge: DiGi Age robots may apply FxL=D (facts times law equals decision) and dura lex, sed lex automatically -- but 'only humans have a heart, only humans have wisdom, only humans can dispense compassionate justice especially when the law is not clear, when the law is inadequate, or when the law is unconscionable.' He commissions the scholars as 'the leaders of the DiGi generation' in 10-20 years, closing with the hovering-spirit promise: 'my spirit will be hovering above you, beside you and behind you, smiling and contented, that I have brought you a few little things that have made a vital difference.'

Timeline: Election Day (May 10) to GMA's term end (June 30) = 61 days. 'Many things can happen during that period.' Closes with Einstein: 'Insanity is committing the same errors and expecting different results.'
